title: System design
audience: Has built or worked on a web application or an API
Wants to design systems that hold up under load and failure

outcomes.description: Turn a vague request into requirements, and work from a simple design towards the first bottleneck.
Estimate requests per second, storage and bandwidth with rounded arithmetic.
Choose between scaling up and scaling out, and find the state that stops an application from running as many copies.
Choose a data store from the questions the system asks of its data.
Design a cache with keys, expiry and invalidation, and protect it against a stampede and a cold start.
Set up leader and follower copies, handle replication lag, and say what failover and backups each protect against.
Choose a partition key from the access patterns, and name what partitioning takes away.
Decide which data needs strong consistency and which can be eventual, and prevent conflicting writes.
Move work out of a request onto a queue, with workers that are safe to repeat.
Tell a command from an event, and publish events reliably with an outbox.
Find how a failure spreads through a design, and contain it with timeouts, breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks.
Set availability and recovery targets as numbers, and choose redundancy that meets them.
Choose metrics, logs and traces for a service, and alert on what users experience.
Protect a system past its limit with rate limits, load shedding and backpressure.
Follow a complete design from requirements to trade-offs, and revise it when a requirement changes.
Review a flawed design and produce one for a new problem, without help.

lessons.title: How to approach a design
lessons.intro: System design is deciding which parts a system needs and how they work together, before the code is written. This module gives you an order to work in, so that a large, vague request becomes a series of small decisions.

steps.title: What a design is for
steps.text:
A design answers three questions.

1. **What must the system do?** The features, stated exactly.
2. **How well must it do them?** How many users, how fast, how reliable.
3. **What will it cost?** In machines, in complexity and in work to run it.

Every design is a set of **trade-offs**: choices where gaining one thing costs another. A cache makes reads faster and makes data possibly out of date. A second copy of the database survives a failure and has to be kept in step. There is no best design in general. There is a design that fits these requirements at this size.

A common mistake is to design for a size the system will never reach. A system for 500 users does not need what a system for 50 million needs, and building it anyway costs months and adds parts that can fail.

steps.title: The order to work in
steps.text:
Use the same five steps each time.

1. **Requirements.** What it must do, and what is out of scope.
2. **Numbers.** How much traffic and data, roughly.
3. **Interface and data.** The operations it offers and the records it stores.
4. **A simple design.** The fewest parts that could work.
5. **Pressure.** Find what breaks first as load grows or parts fail, and change only that.

The order matters. Without step 1 you solve the wrong problem. Without step 2 you cannot tell whether one machine is enough. Starting at step 5, with queues and shards, before a simple design exists is the usual way designs go wrong.

steps.title: Two kinds of requirement
steps.text:
**Functional requirements** say what the system does: "a user can upload a photo", "a user sees photos from people they follow".

**Non-functional requirements** say how well: how fast, how available, how much data may be lost, how consistent. They decide the shape of the design far more than the features do. Ask about each of these.

| Question | Why it changes the design |
| --- | --- |
| How many users and requests? | One machine or many |
| Mostly reads or mostly writes? | Caches and replicas help reads, not writes |
| How fast must a response be? | Whether work can be done later, in the background |
| How much downtime is acceptable? | How much redundancy to pay for |
| May data be slightly out of date? | Whether caches and replicas can be used at all |
| May any data be lost? | How writes are confirmed and backed up |

Write the answers down as numbers where you can. "Fast" is not a requirement. "95% of page loads under 300 ms" is.

steps.title: Which requirement shapes it
steps.text: Two teams build a "like" button. Team A's product is a company intranet with 2,000 employees. Team B's product is a public app where one post can receive 50,000 likes in a minute.

steps.title: Start with the simplest thing
steps.text:
The simplest design for most systems is the same: clients, one application server, one database. Draw that first.

It is a real design, and it goes further than people expect. One modern server handles thousands of simple requests per second. One database holds hundreds of gigabytes without special effort. Many successful products ran on this shape for years.

Starting simple has a second benefit. It gives you something to test against the numbers. Each part you add later then has a reason: "the database cannot keep up with reads, so add a cache". A part with no stated reason should not be in the drawing.

steps.title: Find the bottleneck
steps.text:
A **bottleneck** is the part that limits the whole system. Work flows only as fast as the slowest step allows, so improving any other part changes nothing.

To find it, follow one request through the design and ask of each part: how much can this handle, and how much will it get? The first part where the load exceeds the capacity is the bottleneck. Fix it, then look again, because the next one is now exposed.

Different systems hit different limits first.

- A system with heavy reads usually runs out of database read capacity.
- A system with heavy writes runs out of disk or of a single writer.
- A system that stores large files runs out of storage and bandwidth.
- A system that does long calculations runs out of processor time.

steps.title: Where to look first
steps.text: A recipe site has 2 million page views a day. Almost every view reads a recipe. About 500 recipes are added or edited per day. Pages are slow in the evening peak.

steps.title: Say what you gave up
steps.text:
A design is easier to judge, and to change later, when each decision is written with its cost.

- "Recipes are cached for 5 minutes. An edit can take 5 minutes to appear."
- "One database, no standby. If it fails, the site is down until a backup is restored, which takes about an hour."
- "Search covers titles only, not the full text."

These sentences are the most useful part of a design document. They tell the next person what was chosen on purpose, and they turn a later complaint into a known trade-off that can be revisited when the requirements change.

steps.title: Exercise: ask before you draw
steps.text: You are asked to "design a system for sharing files inside a company". Before drawing anything, write the questions you would ask. Aim for at least eight. Group them into what the system must do, and how well it must do it. Then state the two answers that would change the design the most.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**What it must do**

1. Who can see a file: only people it is shared with, a team, or everyone in the company?
2. Can files be edited, or only replaced? Are old versions kept?
3. Is there search, and over names only or over contents?
4. Are there folders, links to share, or expiry dates?

**How well**

5. How many employees, and how many files per person?
6. How large is a typical file, and the largest allowed?
7. How quickly must a new file be available to others?
8. How much downtime is acceptable during working hours?
9. May a file ever be lost? For how long are deleted files kept?
10. Are there rules about where the data is stored or who may read it?

**The two that change the most**

- **File size and count** (5 and 6). A thousand people with small documents fit on one storage service with no special design. Video files of several gigabytes mean uploads in parts, transfer that can resume, and a real storage bill.
- **Versions and editing** (2). Replace-only is simple storage. Keeping versions, or letting two people edit one file, brings in conflict handling, which is a much harder problem.

The point of the exercise is that the picture cannot be drawn yet. Two systems that fit the one-line request can differ by a factor of a hundred in size and in difficulty.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason the two designs differ?

choices.text: The feature is different
choices.feedback: Both do the same thing: record that a user liked a post, and show a count.

choices.text: The load is different
choices.feedback: For team A, one database row per like and a count query is enough. For team B, 50,000 writes a minute to one counter needs a different approach.

choices.text: Team B has better engineers
choices.feedback: The requirements decide the design. A good engineer on team A builds the simple version.

questions.prompt: Which change is most likely to help?

choices.text: Make writes faster with a queue
choices.feedback: There are 500 writes a day. Writes are not the load.

choices.text: Reduce the read load on the database, for example with a cache
choices.feedback: Reads outnumber writes 4,000 to 1, and a recipe changes rarely, so a stored copy can serve most views.

choices.text: Split the data across several databases
choices.feedback: That is a large change aimed at data size or write volume, and neither is the problem here.

lessons.title: Estimate load and size
lessons.intro: Before choosing parts, you need rough numbers: how many requests arrive each second, and how much data piles up. This module shows how to get them in a few minutes with rounded arithmetic.

steps.title: Why rough numbers are enough
steps.text:
An estimate does not need to be right. It needs to be right within a factor of about ten, because design decisions change at those jumps. One server or ten. A database on one disk or data spread over many machines.

So round hard. Use 100,000 seconds in a day, not 86,400. Use powers of ten. An estimate you can do in your head is more useful than a precise one that takes an hour, since its inputs are guesses anyway.

Write the assumptions down next to the result. When the real numbers arrive, you can swap them in and see whether any decision changes.

steps.title: Requests per second
steps.text:
Start from users and work down.

1. **Daily active users**: how many people use the system on a normal day.
2. **Actions per user per day**: how often each one does the thing.
3. Multiply to get requests per day.
4. Divide by 100,000 to get the average **requests per second** (often written RPS or QPS, for queries per second).

Traffic is not even. Most systems have a daily peak of two to five times the average, and some have rare spikes far above that. Design for the peak. The average is what you pay for and the peak is what breaks you.

steps.title: Reads and writes
steps.text:
Split the number into reads and writes, because they stress different parts. Reads can be served from copies and caches. Writes must reach the one place that holds the truth.

Most systems are **read-heavy**. A social feed might be read a hundred times for every post written. A few are **write-heavy**, such as systems that collect measurements from sensors or record every click.

The ratio tells you where to spend effort. With 100 reads per write, anything that makes reads cheaper pays off 100 times over.

steps.title: Storage
steps.text:
Estimate storage the same way.

1. How many new records per day?
2. How large is one record?
3. Multiply, then multiply by the number of days you keep them.

Sizes to remember, rounded:

| Thing | Size |
| --- | --- |
| A short text record (a comment, an order line) | about 1 KB |
| A row with a few numbers and IDs | about 100 bytes |
| A compressed photo | about 1 MB |
| One minute of compressed video | about 10 to 50 MB |

And the units: 1,000 KB is 1 MB, 1,000 MB is 1 GB, 1,000 GB is 1 TB.

Copies multiply the result. If the data is kept three times for safety, plus backups, the disk needed is several times the raw figure.

steps.title: Which is larger
steps.text: A photo app has 100,000 users who each upload 5 photos a day at 2 MB per photo. Each photo also has a database row of 500 bytes with its owner, date and caption.

steps.title: What one machine can do
steps.text:
To turn load into a machine count you need a feel for capacity. These are rough figures for ordinary hardware. They vary widely with the work being done.

| Part | Rough capacity |
| --- | --- |
| A web server doing simple requests | 1,000 or more requests per second |
| A relational database, simple indexed reads | several thousand per second |
| A relational database, writes | hundreds to a few thousand per second |
| An in-memory cache | 100,000 or more operations per second |
| One disk | several TB |

Use them to sanity-check, not to plan exactly. If the estimate says 600 requests per second at peak, one server can do the work and you want two so that one can fail. If it says 60,000, you need many servers and the database becomes the real question.

steps.title: Bandwidth and memory
steps.text:
Two more quick estimates are sometimes needed.

**Bandwidth** is requests per second multiplied by response size. 600 requests per second of 50 KB pages is 30 MB per second. That is fine for a data centre connection and a reason to compress responses and move images to a CDN.

**Memory for a cache** follows from what you want to keep. A common rule is that a small share of the items gets most of the requests. Caching the most popular 20% of 10 million records of 1 KB each needs about 2 GB, which fits in one machine.

steps.title: Latency numbers worth knowing
steps.text:
Some operations are thousands of times slower than others. The order matters more than the exact values.

| Operation | Rough time |
| --- | --- |
| Read from memory | under a microsecond |
| Read from a fast local disk | about 0.1 ms |
| A call to another machine in the same data centre | about 0.5 ms |
| A simple database query, with an index | 1 to 5 ms |
| A call across a continent | 40 to 80 ms |
| A call between continents | 100 to 300 ms |

One conclusion follows at once. A request that makes 50 database calls one after another spends 50 to 250 ms on waiting alone. Counting the calls a design makes per request is part of estimating it.

steps.title: The spike
steps.text: A ticket site averages 50 requests per second. When tickets for a popular concert go on sale, 200,000 people open the page within the same minute.

steps.title: Exercise: size a system
steps.text:
A team plans a service for short voice notes. Assume 2 million daily active users. Each sends 10 notes a day and listens to 40. A note is 20 seconds long and takes 100 KB. Each note has a 200-byte record. Notes are kept for one year.

Estimate: the average and peak requests per second for sending and for listening, the storage for the audio and for the records after a year, and the peak download bandwidth. State which of these numbers should worry the team most.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Requests**

| | Per day | Average per second | Peak (x 3) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Send | 20 million | 200 | 600 |
| Listen | 80 million | 800 | 2,400 |

**Storage after a year**

- Audio: 20 million notes a day at 100 KB is 2 TB a day, or about 800 TB a year. With three copies, about 2.4 PB (1 PB is 1,000 TB).
- Records: 20 million a day at 200 bytes is 4 GB a day, or about 1.6 TB a year.

**Bandwidth at peak**

2,400 downloads per second at 100 KB is 240 MB per second.

**What to worry about**

The request rates are modest. A handful of servers handle 3,000 requests per second. The record data fits in one large database, with some care.

The audio storage is the problem. It is 500 times larger than the records, it grows by 2 TB every day, and its cost continues for as long as notes are kept. It decides the main choices: audio goes to object storage and never into the database, downloads go through a CDN, and the one-year retention rule is worth questioning, since halving it halves the bill.

This is what an estimate is for. It took a few minutes, and it showed which part of the system deserves the design effort.

choices.feedback: 200,000 in 60 seconds is about 3,300 per second, before anyone refreshes the page. A design sized for the daily peak fails here.

lessons.title: Scale up and scale out
lessons.intro: When one server is no longer enough, there are two ways to get more capacity. This module covers both, what has to be true of an application before it can run on many machines, and how machines are added and removed automatically.

steps.title: Two directions
steps.text:
**Scaling up** (vertical scaling) means replacing a machine with a larger one: more processors, more memory, faster disks.

**Scaling out** (horizontal scaling) means adding more machines of the same size and spreading the work across them.

| | Scale up | Scale out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change to the application | None | It must work as many copies |
| Limit | The largest machine you can buy | Almost none for stateless work |
| Cost at the high end | Rises steeply | Rises in proportion |
| Failure of one machine | Total outage | Lose a share of capacity |
| Effort to operate | Low | Higher: many machines, a load balancer |

Scaling up is the right first move more often than its reputation suggests. It needs no redesign, and a single large machine is simple to run. Its two real limits are the ceiling and the fact that one machine is one point of failure.

steps.title: What "stateless" means
steps.text:
Scaling out puts several copies of the application behind a load balancer. Any request may reach any copy. That works only if every copy can answer every request, which means no copy may keep information that another copy would need.

**State** is anything the system must remember between requests: who is logged in, what is in a shopping cart, an uploaded file, a counter. An application is **stateless** when it keeps none of that in its own memory or on its own disk. All state lives in a shared place that every copy can reach: a database, a cache or file storage.

A stateless copy can be started, stopped or replaced at any moment without anything being lost. That one property is what makes the rest of this module possible.

steps.title: Where state hides
steps.text:
State often sits in the application without anyone having decided it should.

| Hidden state | What goes wrong with several copies | Where it belongs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Login sessions in memory | The user is logged out when a request reaches another copy | A shared cache or a signed token |
| Uploaded files on local disk | The file exists on one copy only | Object storage |
| An in-memory cache of data | Copies disagree after an update | A shared cache, or accept short-lived differences |
| A counter or a rate limit in memory | Each copy counts separately | A shared store |
| A scheduled job inside the app | It runs once per copy | One scheduler, or a lock |

The last row surprises people. An application that sends a daily report at 08:00 will send three reports when it runs as three copies.

steps.title: The upload that vanished
steps.text: A site runs as three copies behind a load balancer. A user uploads a profile photo, which the application saves to a folder on its local disk. The page then reloads and requests the photo.

steps.title: The database does not scale out the same way
steps.text:
Application servers are easy to copy because they hold no state. The database is the opposite: it is where the state lives. Ten copies of a database are ten databases that disagree, unless something keeps them in step.

So the usual picture is many application servers and one database, and the database is scaled up for as long as possible. When that is no longer enough, there are specific techniques, each with a cost, and each has its own module later in the course.

- **Caching** takes repeated reads away from the database.
- **Replication** adds copies that can serve reads.
- **Partitioning** splits the data across several databases.

Try them in that order. Each one is harder than the one before.

steps.title: Adding machines automatically
steps.text:
Traffic changes through the day. Running enough machines for the evening peak all night wastes money. **Autoscaling** adds copies when load rises and removes them when it falls.

You give it three things.

- A **signal** to watch, such as average processor use or requests per copy.
- A **target** for that signal, such as 60%.
- A **minimum and maximum** number of copies.

Three details decide whether it works in practice.

- **Start-up time.** If a new copy needs four minutes to be ready, it cannot help with a spike that lasts two. Keep copies quick to start, and keep some spare capacity for sudden jumps.
- **The minimum.** Never fewer than two, so one can fail.
- **Removal.** A copy that is being removed must finish its current requests first. This is the draining described in the networking course.

steps.title: Capacity and spare room
steps.text:
How many copies are enough? Take the peak load, divide by what one copy can handle, and then add room for failure.

A useful rule is to plan for losing one copy, or one location, at the worst moment. If the peak needs four copies, run five or six, so that the loss of one does not push the others over their limit. Without that room, one failure overloads the rest, and they fail in turn. That chain is called a **cascading failure**.

steps.title: Enough copies
steps.text: A service needs 6 copies to carry its peak. The team runs exactly 6, split evenly over 3 zones (independent locations in one region). One zone loses power at the peak.

steps.title: Exercise: make it scale out
steps.text:
An application runs on one server. It does these things:

1. Keeps login sessions in memory.
2. Stores uploaded invoices as files in `/var/data/invoices`.
3. Keeps a list of the 100 most-viewed products in memory, refreshed every 10 minutes.
4. Runs a job every night at 02:00 that emails unpaid-invoice reminders.
5. Limits each user to 5 login attempts per minute, counted in memory.

The team wants to run four copies behind a load balancer. For each of the five, say what breaks and what you would change. Say which one could be left as it is.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Sessions.** A user is logged out whenever a request lands on another copy. Move sessions to a shared cache, or use signed tokens that any copy can check.
2. **Invoice files.** A file exists on one copy only, and is lost when that copy is replaced. Move the files to object storage, and store only their location in the database.
3. **Top products.** Each copy builds its own list, and they may differ slightly for a few minutes. This one can stay. The data is not critical, and a small difference between copies does no harm. It costs four queries every 10 minutes, not one.
4. **Nightly job.** Every copy runs it, so each customer gets four reminders. Run the job in one place: a separate scheduled task outside the web copies, or guard it with a lock in the database so only one copy proceeds.
5. **Login limit.** Each copy counts on its own, so the real limit becomes 20 attempts a minute, spread by the load balancer. Count in a shared store.

Point 3 is the lesson worth keeping. Not all in-memory state is a fault. The question for each piece is: what happens when two copies disagree about it? If the answer is "nothing that matters", leave it alone.

lessons.title: Choose a data store
lessons.intro: Where data lives decides what the system can do quickly, what it can guarantee and how it grows. This module covers the main kinds of data store and how to choose by asking how the data will be read.

steps.title: Start from the questions, not the product
steps.text:
A data store is good at some questions and bad at others. So the first step is to list the questions the system will ask of its data. These are called **access patterns**.

- "Get the order with this ID."
- "List this customer's orders, newest first."
- "Find products whose description mentions 'waterproof'."
- "Total sales per region for last month."

Each one favours a different kind of store. Choosing a product first and discovering the questions later is how systems end up with a store that cannot answer what they need.

steps.title: Relational databases
steps.text:
A **relational database** keeps data in tables of rows and columns, with a fixed structure, and is queried with SQL. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server are examples.

Its strengths are broad.

- It answers questions nobody planned for, by joining and filtering tables.
- It enforces rules: a required column, a unique email, an order that must refer to a real customer.
- It supports **transactions**: a group of changes that all happen or none do. Moving money between two accounts is the standard example.

Its limit is scale in one direction. All of this works best on one machine, and spreading a relational database over many machines is hard.

Use a relational database by default. It fits most data, it protects you from many mistakes, and it carries a system a long way. Choose something else when you can name the specific thing it cannot do for you.

steps.title: Key-value stores
steps.text:
A **key-value store** does one thing: give it a key and it returns the value stored under that key. It cannot search inside values or join anything. Redis and Memcached keep the data in memory. Others, such as DynamoDB, keep it on disk and spread it across many machines.

Since every operation names one key, the store always knows which machine holds the data. That makes it very fast and easy to spread out.

It fits sessions, caches, counters, feature settings and anything looked up by one identifier. It does not fit data you need to query in several ways.

steps.title: Document stores
steps.text:
A **document store** keeps each record as a self-contained document, usually in a JSON-like form, and lets you query by fields inside it. MongoDB is an example.

A document can hold nested data that a relational design would split across several tables: an order together with its lines and its delivery address. Reading the whole thing is one lookup, and records need not all have the same fields.

The cost appears when data is shared between documents. If each order document holds a copy of the customer's name, changing the name means updating every order. Relational databases avoid this by storing each fact once. Document stores fit data that is read and written as a whole and rarely needs joining.

steps.title: Object storage
steps.text:
**Object storage** holds files of any size under a name: images, videos, backups, exports, logs. Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage are examples. You upload a file, get it back by name and delete it. There are no queries.

It is cheap per gigabyte, it grows without limit, and it keeps several copies for you. It is slower per request than a database, which does not matter for large files.

The rule is simple: files do not belong in a database. Store the file in object storage and store its name, size and owner as a row in the database.

steps.title: Where does it go
steps.text: A team stores scanned contracts as PDF files of about 5 MB each, inside a column of their relational database. They have 2 million contracts.

steps.title: Search indexes and other special stores
steps.text:
Some questions need a store built for them.

- A **search index**, such as Elasticsearch, answers "which documents contain these words?" quickly, with ranking and tolerance for typing errors. A database's `LIKE '%word%'` reads every row.
- A **time-series database** is built for measurements with a timestamp: store millions of points, query a range, compute averages over intervals.
- A **data warehouse** is built for analysis: totals and trends over years of data. It stores data by column, which makes sums over one column fast and single-row lookups slow.
- A **graph database** is built for following connections: friends of friends, routes, dependencies.

These are usually second stores. The main database stays the source of truth, and a copy of the relevant data is sent to the special store. That copy lags a little, and you must keep it in step. It is a real cost, so add a special store when a need is proven, not in advance.

steps.title: Indexes
steps.text:
Whatever the store, one idea decides read speed. An **index** is an extra structure that lets the store find rows by a column without reading the whole table, like the index at the back of a book.

Without an index on `customer_id`, "list this customer's orders" reads every order. With one, it goes straight to the matching rows.

Indexes are not free. Each one takes space and must be updated on every write, so a table with ten indexes is slower to write. Add an index for each question the system asks often, and no more.

steps.title: More than one store
steps.text:
Real systems often use several stores, each for what it does best.


Decide for each piece of data which store is the **source of truth**: the one place whose value is correct when two stores disagree. Everything else is a copy that can be rebuilt from it.

steps.title: Which store
steps.text: A site needs "search products by words in the name and description, with results ranked by relevance, tolerating small typing errors". The products are in a relational database of 3 million rows.

steps.title: Exercise: place the data
steps.text:
A ride-booking service has these kinds of data. For each, choose a store and give one sentence of reasoning.

1. Rider and driver accounts.
2. Each trip: rider, driver, start, end, price, payment status.
3. The current location of every active driver, updated every 4 seconds.
4. Photos of drivers' licences.
5. "Find trips whose notes mention a lost item."
6. Total revenue per city per week, for the finance team.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Relational database.** Accounts need unique emails, rules and joins with trips.
2. **Relational database.** A trip and its payment must change together in a transaction, and trips are queried in many ways.
3. **In-memory key-value store.** One value per driver, overwritten every few seconds, read constantly, and worthless a minute later. Writing it to the main database would be thousands of pointless writes per second. If it is lost, it refills within seconds.
4. **Object storage**, with a row in the database for the owner and the file's name. Access must be restricted, since these are identity documents.
5. **Search index**, fed from the trip notes. If this is a rare support task, a slow database query might be enough, and a whole new store would not be worth running.
6. **Data warehouse**, or at a small size a scheduled query against a copy of the database. Either way, not the live database at peak time.

Two answers deserve a second look. Number 3 shows that how often data changes and how long it matters can decide the store. Number 5 shows that "which store fits best" and "is it worth adding" are separate questions.

choices.text: Add an ordinary index on the description column

lessons.title: Caches
lessons.intro: A cache keeps a copy of an answer so that the work of producing it is not repeated. It is the most common way to make a system faster, and the most common source of out-of-date data. This module covers how a cache is used, how entries leave it, and how caches fail.

steps.title: What a cache is
steps.text:
A **cache** is a store of results, kept somewhere fast, usually in memory. When the same question is asked again, the answer comes from the cache and the slow source is not touched.

Two terms describe what happens on a lookup.

- A **hit**: the answer was in the cache.
- A **miss**: it was not, so the source is asked and the result is usually stored for next time.

The **hit rate** is the share of lookups that are hits. A cache with a 95% hit rate removes 95% of the load from whatever is behind it. A cache with a 20% hit rate adds a lookup to most requests and saves little.

A cache pays off when data is read much more often than it changes, and when a small part of the data gets most of the requests.

steps.title: Where caches sit
steps.text:
Caches exist at every level between the user and the data, and a request may pass several.


The closer to the user a hit happens, the more work is saved. A hit in the browser costs no network traffic at all. This module is mostly about the application cache, since it is the one you design. The same rules apply at every level.

steps.title: Cache-aside
steps.text:
The usual way to use an application cache is called **cache-aside**. The application talks to both the cache and the database.

To read:

1. Look in the cache.
2. On a hit, return the value.
3. On a miss, read the database, store the value in the cache, and return it.

To write:

1. Update the database.
2. Delete the entry from the cache.

The next read misses and loads the new value. Deleting is safer than writing the new value into the cache. If two updates happen at almost the same time, writing can leave the older value in the cache. A delete cannot leave a wrong value behind.

steps.title: Entries have to leave
steps.text:
A cache has limited memory, and its copies go out of date. Two mechanisms remove entries.

**Expiry.** Each entry gets a **TTL** (time to live), such as 5 minutes. After that it is dropped, and the next read fetches a fresh value. The TTL is a direct trade: a longer one means more hits and older data.

**Eviction.** When memory is full, something must go to make room. The usual policy is **LRU** (least recently used): drop the entry that has gone longest without being read.

A TTL is also a safety net. If a delete is missed because of a bug or a crash, the wrong value does not stay for ever. Give every entry a TTL, even when you also delete on write.

steps.title: How stale can it be
steps.text: Product prices are cached with a TTL of 10 minutes. The cache entry is not deleted when a price changes. A price is corrected from 5.00 to 50.00 at 12:00.

steps.title: Deciding what may be stale
steps.text:
"The cache may be out of date" is acceptable for some data and not for other data. Decide for each kind.

| Data | Stale for a minute? |
| --- | --- |
| A product description | Fine |
| The number of likes on a post | Fine |
| A list of search results | Fine |
| The stock count shown on a product page | Usually fine, if checkout checks the real value |
| An account balance used to approve a payment | No |
| Whether a user's access was revoked | No, or only for a very short time |

The pattern in the fourth row is common. Show a cached value where a small error does no harm, and read the real value at the moment a decision is made.

steps.title: The stampede
steps.text:
A popular entry expires. In the next instant, 500 requests arrive, all miss, and all run the same slow query at once. The database, which the cache was protecting, receives 500 copies of its most expensive query. This is a **cache stampede**.

Three defences are common.

- **One loader.** On a miss, the first request takes a short lock and fetches the value. The others wait briefly for it or are given the old value.
- **Refresh before expiry.** A background job reloads popular entries before their TTL runs out, so users never see a miss.
- **Spread the expiry times.** Add a random amount to each TTL. Entries that were all stored at once, after a restart for example, then do not all expire in the same second.

steps.title: When the cache is empty or gone
steps.text:
A cache also changes how the system fails.

A **cold cache** is an empty one, after a restart or a deploy. Every request is a miss until it fills. If the database can only cope because the cache normally absorbs 95% of the reads, a cold cache means twenty times the usual database load, at once.

So test one thing on purpose: can the system survive with an empty cache? If not, the cache is no longer an optimisation. It is a required part of the system, and it needs the same care as the database: more than one copy, monitoring, and a plan for filling it gradually.

Two more rules follow from this.

- **A cache failure should not be an outage.** If the cache cannot be reached, fall back to the database, with a limit on how much load is let through.
- **Never make the cache the only copy.** Anything in it must be recoverable from the source of truth.

steps.title: Keys and what goes in them
steps.text:
A cache entry is found by its key, so the key must contain everything the answer depends on. If a page differs by user language, the language belongs in the key. If it differs by user, the user ID does.

Leaving something out is a serious bug. A key of `account-page` with no user ID serves one person's account page to the next visitor. When a cached response contains anything personal, check the key first.

steps.title: A cold start
steps.text: A system serves 10,000 reads per second. Its cache has a 98% hit rate. The database handles up to 1,000 reads per second. The cache servers are restarted during the evening peak.

steps.title: Exercise: design the caching
steps.text:
A news site has 5,000 articles. An article page shows the article text, a comment count, and a "most read today" list of ten links. Articles are edited rarely, though a correction must be visible within one minute. Comment counts change constantly. The site gets 3,000 page views per second at peak, and one front-page article can take half of them.

Decide what to cache, with which key and TTL, and what happens on an edit. Say how you would protect against a stampede on the front-page article.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
| Entry | Key | TTL | On change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Article text | `article:{id}` | 10 minutes | Delete on edit |
| Comment count | `comments:count:{id}` | 30 seconds | Nothing. Let it expire |
| Most read today | `most-read` | 60 seconds | Nothing. Recomputed on expiry |

**Edits.** Deleting the entry on edit makes a correction visible on the next request, well within one minute. The 10-minute TTL is the safety net for a missed delete, and it bounds the delay at 10 minutes in that rare case. If one minute must hold even then, lower the TTL to 60 seconds. At this traffic the hit rate stays above 99%.

**Comment counts.** A count that is 30 seconds old is harmless, and deleting the entry on every comment would defeat the cache for a busy article.

**Stampede.** The front-page article gets 1,500 requests per second. When its entry expires, use one loader: the first request reloads it and the rest are served the previous copy for the moment that takes. Refreshing it in the background before expiry works as well.

The whole page could also be cached at the CDN for 30 to 60 seconds. For a news site where every reader sees the same page, that removes most requests before they reach the application at all.

choices.feedback: The data is still in the database. The problem is the load.

lessons.title: Replication
lessons.intro: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines. It protects against losing a machine and adds capacity for reads. This module covers the usual arrangement, the delay it introduces, and what happens when the main copy fails.

steps.title: Why keep copies
steps.text:
A database on one machine has two problems. If the machine fails, the system is down, and data written since the last backup may be gone. And one machine can serve only so many reads.

**Replication** addresses both. Each copy is called a **replica**. With replicas you get:

- **Availability.** Another copy can take over when one fails.
- **Durability.** Data survives the loss of a disk or a machine.
- **Read capacity.** Reads can be spread across the copies.
- **Distance.** A copy can be placed near users in another region.

Replication does not increase write capacity. Every write must still be applied to every copy.

steps.title: Leader and followers
steps.text:
The most common arrangement has one **leader** (also called the primary) and one or more **followers** (also called replicas or secondaries).

- All writes go to the leader.
- The leader records each change in a log and sends it to the followers.
- Each follower applies the changes in the same order.
- Reads may go to the leader or to any follower.

One writer keeps things simple. There is a single order of changes, so two copies never have to settle a conflict.

steps.title: Synchronous or asynchronous
steps.text:
When the leader receives a write, it can confirm it to the application at two different moments.

**Synchronous.** The leader waits until a follower confirms that it has the change, and only then answers. The data exists in two places before the application is told "saved". The cost is speed, and if the follower is slow or unreachable, writes wait.

**Asynchronous.** The leader answers as soon as it has saved the change itself, and sends it to the followers afterwards. Writes are fast and do not depend on the followers. The cost is a window in which the change exists on the leader only. If the leader dies in that window, the change is lost, although the application was told it was saved.

Many systems use a mix: one follower is synchronous, so every confirmed write is on two machines, and the rest are asynchronous.

| | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Write speed | Slower | Faster |
| A confirmed write can be lost | No | Yes, if the leader fails at the wrong moment |
| A slow follower | Slows writes | Affects nothing |

steps.title: Replication lag
steps.text:
With asynchronous replication, a follower is always slightly behind the leader. This delay is **replication lag**. It is normally a fraction of a second. Under heavy write load, or when a follower is busy, it can grow to seconds or minutes.

Lag produces a specific and confusing bug. A user saves a change, which goes to the leader. The page reloads and reads from a follower that does not have the change yet. The user sees the old value and concludes that the save failed.

steps.title: Reading your own writes
steps.text:
The fix is a guarantee called **read-your-writes**: a user always sees their own changes, even if other users see them a moment later. There are several ways to provide it.

- Read from the leader for a short time after a user writes, such as 10 seconds.
- Read from the leader for data that only its owner edits, such as a user's own profile and settings.
- Remember the position in the change log of the user's last write, and read only from a follower that has reached it.

Other users seeing the change half a second late is nearly always fine. What must not happen is a person failing to see what they just did.

steps.title: After the save
steps.text: A forum sends all reads to followers, which lag by about 2 seconds at busy times. A user posts a reply and is taken to the thread page.

steps.title: When the leader fails
steps.text:
If a follower fails, reads move to the others and little is lost. If the leader fails, nothing can be written until a follower takes its place. That change is called **failover**. It has three steps.

1. **Detect** that the leader is gone, usually by a missed heartbeat for some seconds.
2. **Promote** a follower to be the new leader, preferably the one that is most up to date.
3. **Redirect** writes to the new leader, and make the other followers follow it.

Each step can go wrong.

- **Lost writes.** With asynchronous replication, changes that never reached the promoted follower are gone.
- **False alarms.** A leader that is slow, not dead, may be declared failed. If the limit is too short, failovers happen for no reason. If it is too long, real outages last longer.
- **Two leaders.** If the old leader comes back and still believes it is the leader, both accept writes and the data diverges. This is called **split brain**, and it is the worst outcome. Systems prevent it by making sure the old leader is shut out before the new one starts.

Managed database services automate failover. It still takes time, often 30 seconds to a few minutes, and applications must reconnect and retry.

steps.title: More than one leader
steps.text:
Some systems allow writes on several nodes: **multi-leader** setups, used across regions, and **leaderless** stores, where a write is sent to several nodes and counts as saved when enough of them confirm it.

They keep accepting writes when a node or a region is cut off. The price is **conflicts**: two nodes can accept different changes to the same record at the same time, and something must decide the result. The simplest rule, "the last write wins", silently throws one of the changes away.

Choose these only when you need writes to continue in several regions and can say how each conflict is settled. For most systems, one leader is the right design.

steps.title: Backups are still needed
steps.text:
Replication copies every change, including the wrong ones. If someone deletes a table by mistake, the delete reaches every follower within a second.

A **backup** is a copy from a point in the past, kept apart from the running system. It protects against the things replication repeats faithfully: mistakes, bugs and deliberate damage. A system needs both. And a backup that has never been restored in a test is a hope, not a backup.

steps.title: What survives
steps.text: A database has a leader and two followers, all asynchronous. At 14:00 an engineer runs a command on the leader that deletes all rows from the `orders` table by mistake.

steps.title: Exercise: choose the setup
steps.text:
A clinic booking system stores appointments. It has 300 writes and 6,000 reads per minute. A confirmed booking must never be lost. Patients must see their own booking at once. The clinic can accept about two minutes of downtime if a machine fails, and must be able to recover if staff delete data by mistake.

Describe the replication setup: the number of copies, which are synchronous, where reads go, how failover works and what backups are kept.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Copies.** One leader and two followers, in three separate zones.

**Synchronous or not.** One follower is synchronous. A booking is confirmed only when it is on two machines in two zones, so a confirmed booking survives the loss of the leader. The second follower is asynchronous, so that a slow machine there cannot hold up writes.

**Reads.** The load is small: 100 reads per second. The leader could serve all of it. Send a patient's own bookings to the leader, which gives read-your-writes with no extra mechanism, and send staff schedule views and reports to the followers.

**Failover.** Automatic, and promoting the synchronous follower, since it has every confirmed write. With detection after about 30 seconds and promotion after that, it fits the two-minute allowance. The application retries connections with backoff.

**Backups.** A full backup every night and the change log kept continuously, so the data can be restored to any minute. Test a restore on a schedule.

A simpler answer is worth saying out loud. At this load, the replicas exist for safety and availability, not for capacity. Routing reads to followers adds the lag problem and solves nothing the system has. Using followers only as standbys would be a reasonable design.

lessons.title: Partitioning
lessons.intro: When the data or the write load no longer fits on one machine, it has to be split. This module covers how data is divided, how the choice of key decides everything that follows, and what splitting takes away.

steps.title: What partitioning is
steps.text:
**Partitioning** splits one large set of data into smaller sets that live on different machines. Each piece is a **partition** or a **shard**, and splitting a database this way is called **sharding**.

Replication and partitioning solve different problems, and large systems use both.

- Replication keeps the same data on several machines. It helps reads and survives failures.
- Partitioning puts different data on different machines. It helps writes and total size.

Each partition is normally replicated too, so every shard has its own leader and followers.

steps.title: The partition key
steps.text:
Every record is placed by its **partition key**: one field whose value decides the shard. For a system with many customers it is often the customer ID.

The key is the most important decision in a partitioned design, and it is hard to change afterwards. A good key does two things.

- It **spreads the data and the load evenly** across the shards.
- It **keeps data that is used together on the same shard**, so the common requests need only one of them.

A request that includes the key goes straight to one shard. A request without it must ask every shard and combine the answers. This is a **scatter-gather** query, and it is slow, costly and only as reliable as the least reliable shard.

So choose the key from the access patterns. If nearly every request is "something for this customer", the customer ID is the key.

steps.title: Two ways to map keys to shards
steps.text:
**By range.** Each shard holds a continuous range of keys: A to H, I to P, Q to Z. Range queries stay cheap, since neighbouring keys sit together. The risk is uneven load. If the key is a date, every new record lands on the last shard, and one machine takes all the writes.

**By hash.** A hash function turns the key into a number that looks random, and the number decides the shard. The load spreads evenly whatever the keys look like. The price is that neighbouring keys end up scattered, so a range query has to ask every shard.

| | By range | By hash |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Even spread | Only if the keys are evenly used | Yes |
| Range queries | One or a few shards | Every shard |
| Typical risk | All new data on one shard | Nothing stays together |

steps.title: Hot keys
steps.text:
Even a perfect spread of keys does not mean an even spread of load. If one key gets far more traffic than the others, the shard that holds it is overloaded while the rest are idle. That key is a **hot key**, and its shard a **hot spot**.

One famous account with millions of followers, one very large customer or one viral post can each be a hot key. Adding shards does not help, since the hot key still lives on exactly one of them.

Ways to deal with it:

- **Cache** the hot item, so most reads never reach the shard.
- **Split the key further**, for example by adding a suffix so one large customer's data is spread over several shards.
- **Give a known large customer a shard of its own.**

steps.title: The date key
steps.text: A system stores sensor readings and partitions them by range on the reading's timestamp, one shard per month. It receives 20,000 new readings per second.

steps.title: Adding shards
steps.text:
Sooner or later a partitioned system needs more shards, and data must move. This is **rebalancing**. How much has to move depends on how keys are mapped.

The naive mapping is `hash(key) mod N`, where N is the number of shards. It is simple and has a serious flaw: when N changes from 4 to 5, the result changes for almost every key, so nearly all the data has to move at once.

Two designs avoid that.

- **Many fixed partitions.** Create far more partitions than machines at the start, for example 1,000 partitions on 4 machines. A key always maps to the same partition. To add a machine, move some whole partitions to it. Only the data in those partitions moves.
- **Consistent hashing.** Keys and machines are placed on the same circle of hash values, and each key belongs to the next machine around the circle. Adding a machine takes over one section of the circle from its neighbour, so only that section's keys move.

Either way, adding the fifth machine moves about a fifth of the data, not all of it.

steps.title: What partitioning takes away
steps.text:
A single database gives you features that stop working across shards, or become slow and complicated.

- **Joins across shards.** The database cannot join rows that live on different machines. The application must fetch from both and combine them.
- **Transactions across shards.** "All or nothing" is easy on one machine and hard across several. It needs a coordination protocol that is slower and can leave things stuck when a machine fails.
- **Unique rules.** "This email is used only once" cannot be checked by one shard when the other emails are elsewhere.
- **Totals and reports.** Any question about all the data is a scatter-gather query.
- **Operations.** Backups, schema changes and upgrades are done once per shard.

This is why partitioning comes last. Scale up, add caches, add read replicas, move old data to an archive and move large files to object storage first. Each of those is cheaper than sharding and can be undone.

steps.title: The email that must be unique
steps.text: A system is partitioned by user ID across 8 shards. It must guarantee that no two accounts share an email address.

steps.title: Exercise: pick the key
steps.text:
A messaging product has 40 million users in 2 million group chats. Messages are 500 bytes on average, and 3 billion are sent per day. The main requests are:

1. Show the latest 50 messages in a chat.
2. Send a message to a chat.
3. Show a user's list of chats with the latest message of each.
4. Search a user's messages for a word. This is rare.

One database can no longer hold the messages. Choose a partition key for the message data, say whether you would map by range or by hash, name the request that suffers, and name one hot-key risk.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Key: the chat ID, mapped by hash.**

Requests 1 and 2 are by far the most frequent, and both name one chat. With the chat ID as the key, all of a chat's messages are on one shard, and each of those requests touches exactly one. Inside the shard, messages are sorted by time, so "the latest 50" reads neighbouring rows.

Hashing is right because chat IDs carry no meaning worth keeping in order, and hashing spreads 2 million chats evenly. Mapping by range on time would send every new message to one shard, as in the sensor example.

**The request that suffers: 3.** A user's chats are spread over many shards. Fetching the latest message of each would be a scatter-gather query on every app open. The usual answer is a second set of data, keyed by user ID, that holds each user's chat list with a preview. It is updated when a message is sent. This stores the same fact twice in exchange for a one-shard read.

Request 4 also crosses shards. Since it is rare, a separate search index fed from the messages is the normal approach.

**Hot key.** One huge chat, such as a company-wide announcement channel with 100,000 members, puts all its traffic on one shard. Its recent messages can be cached, and a known giant can be given its own shard.

The size check: 3 billion messages at 500 bytes is 1.5 TB per day. That confirms the premise. No single machine holds a year of this.

lessons.title: Consistency and its trade-offs
lessons.intro: Once data lives on more than one machine, the copies can disagree for a while. This module covers what "consistent" means, why a system sometimes has to choose between a correct answer and any answer, and how to decide what each piece of data needs.

steps.title: The problem
steps.text:
With one database on one machine, a read returns the latest write. Nothing else is possible, so nobody thinks about it.

With replicas, caches and partitions, there are several copies, and they are updated at slightly different times. A read may now return an older value, depending on which copy answers. **Consistency** is the word for how much of that a system allows.

It is not a matter of right and wrong designs. Stricter consistency costs speed and availability. Looser consistency costs correctness in the moments after a change. The work is to give each kind of data the level it needs and no more.

steps.title: Strong and eventual
steps.text:
Two ends of the range are worth naming.

**Strong consistency.** Every read returns the most recent confirmed write, whichever copy answers. The system behaves like a single machine. To do this, a write is not confirmed until enough copies have it, and a copy that might be behind does not answer reads.

**Eventual consistency.** A write is confirmed quickly and reaches the other copies afterwards. If the writes stop, all copies become the same in the end. In between, different readers may see different values.

| | Strong | Eventual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A read after a write | Always sees it | May see the old value briefly |
| Write speed | Slower, waits for copies | Faster |
| When copies cannot reach each other | Some requests are refused | Keeps answering |
| Fits | Balances, stock at checkout, unique names | Feeds, counters, profiles, search results |

steps.title: Guarantees in between
steps.text:
Most systems need something between the two ends. Three guarantees cover the common cases.

- **Read-your-writes.** A user always sees their own changes. Others may see them later. This removes the "my save was lost" confusion from the replication module.
- **Monotonic reads.** A user never sees time go backwards. Without it, a user can see a new comment, refresh, land on a slower copy and watch the comment vanish. A simple way to get it is to send each user to the same copy every time.
- **Consistent prefix.** Changes are seen in the order they happened. Without it, a reader can see an answer before the question it replies to.

These are far cheaper than strong consistency, and they are usually what people actually want when they say "it must be consistent".

steps.title: Going backwards
steps.text: A user refreshes a discussion page twice. Each refresh is served by a random follower. Follower A is up to date. Follower B is 5 seconds behind. A new reply was posted 2 seconds ago.

steps.title: When the network splits
steps.text:
Machines in a distributed system talk over a network, and networks fail. A **network partition** is a failure in which some machines cannot reach others, although all of them are still running. (This is a different use of the word from data partitioning.)

During a partition, a copy that receives a request cannot check with the other side. It has two choices.

- **Refuse**, because it cannot be sure its data is current. The system stays consistent and is unavailable for that request.
- **Answer anyway**, with what it has. The system stays available and may return old data or accept a write that conflicts with one on the other side.

There is no third choice. This is the **CAP theorem**: when a partition happens, a system can keep consistency or availability, not both. Partitions cannot be ruled out, so the real decision is which of the two to give up while one lasts.

steps.title: Choosing per piece of data
steps.text:
The choice is made per kind of data, not once for the whole system. Ask what a wrong answer costs.

| Data | A stale or conflicting value means | Choose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account balance when approving a payment | Money spent twice | Consistency |
| The last seat on a flight | Two people sold one seat | Consistency |
| A username at sign-up | Two accounts with one name | Consistency |
| Number of likes | A count that is off by a few | Availability |
| A shopping cart | An item that reappears | Availability |
| A product description | An old description for a moment | Availability |

A shop is a good example of mixing both. Browsing and the cart stay available at almost any price, since a refusal loses a sale. The payment step is strict, since a wrong answer costs real money.

steps.title: Transactions
steps.text:
Inside one database, **transactions** give strong guarantees for a group of changes. The usual summary is **ACID**.

- **Atomic.** All of the changes happen, or none.
- **Consistent.** The rules of the data hold afterwards.
- **Isolated.** Transactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-done work.
- **Durable.** Once confirmed, a change survives a crash.

A transfer between two accounts in one database is safe because of this. Take 50 from one, add 50 to the other, and no failure can leave only half done.

Across two databases or two services, there is no such built-in guarantee. That is one more reason to keep data that must change together in the same database.

steps.title: When a change spans services
steps.text:
Sometimes one business action must change data in several services: an order service, a payment service and a stock service. No single transaction covers them.

The usual approach is a **saga**: a sequence of local steps, each a normal transaction in one service, and for each step an undo action, called a **compensation**.

1. Create the order as "pending".
2. Reserve the stock. If that fails, cancel the order.
3. Take the payment. If that fails, release the stock and cancel the order.
4. Mark the order "confirmed".

A saga is not atomic. Between the steps, others can see the in-between state, such as an order that is pending. The design must make those states visible and sensible. That is why real systems show "pending" and "processing", and why they send a correction afterwards when a later step fails.

steps.title: Avoid the conflict
steps.text:
The cheapest way to deal with conflicting writes is to design so that they cannot happen.

- **One writer per piece of data.** If only one service or one leader changes a record, there is nothing to reconcile.
- **Record events, do not overwrite totals.** Store each like as its own row and add them up. Two writers adding rows cannot conflict. Two writers overwriting one counter can.
- **Compare before writing.** Include a version number in an update: "set the price to 12 if the version is still 7". A writer whose copy was old is refused and must read again. This is **optimistic locking**.

steps.title: The last seat
steps.text: A booking system keeps "seats left: 1" for a concert. Two users press "buy" at the same instant. Each request reads the value 1, sees a seat is free, and writes 0.

steps.title: Exercise: assign the level
steps.text:
An online bank's mobile app shows or does these things. For each, say whether it needs strong consistency or can be eventual, and what a user would notice if you chose wrongly.

1. The balance shown on the home screen.
2. The check that a transfer does not exceed the balance.
3. The list of past transactions.
4. A "you spent 12% more on food this month" insight.
5. Freezing a stolen card.
6. The user's own display name after editing it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Eventual, with read-your-writes.** A balance that is a second old is acceptable for viewing. After the user's own transfer, it must show the new figure, or they will think it failed.
2. **Strong.** This is a decision about money. It must read the real balance and decrease it in one transaction. A stale read here lets someone spend the same money twice.
3. **Eventual, with consistent prefix.** A new transaction may appear a moment late. The order must be right, and entries must not appear and vanish.
4. **Eventual.** It can be computed nightly. Nobody is harmed by an insight that is a day old.
5. **Strong.** Every system that approves a payment must see the freeze at once. A copy that has not heard about it yet would approve a thief's purchase. Here the system should refuse payments when it is unsure.
6. **Read-your-writes.** The user must see the new name at once. Others seeing the old one for a second is harmless.

Only two of the six need strong consistency, and both are moments where a decision is made. That ratio is typical. Showing data can usually be eventual. Deciding on data usually cannot.

lessons.title: Queues and background work
lessons.intro: Not every piece of work has to finish before the user gets an answer. A queue lets one part of a system hand work to another and move on. This module covers what a queue gives you, what delivery guarantees mean, and how queues fail.

steps.title: Work now or work later
steps.text:
When a user places an order, some work must finish before the response: check the stock, take the payment, save the order. Other work can happen a moment later: send the confirmation email, update the recommendation data, notify the warehouse.

Doing everything in the request makes it slow and fragile. If the email provider is down, the order fails, although the order itself was fine.

The alternative is to do the required work, put a **message** describing the rest on a **queue**, and respond. Separate programs called **workers** (or consumers) take messages from the queue and do the work. The program that adds messages is the **producer**.

steps.title: What a queue gives you
steps.text:
- **Faster responses.** The user waits only for the work that matters to the answer.
- **Decoupling.** The producer does not need the worker to be running. If the email worker is down for ten minutes, messages wait and are handled when it returns. Nothing is lost and no user sees an error.
- **Levelling the load.** A burst of 10,000 orders in a minute becomes a queue that workers empty at their own steady pace. The queue absorbs the peak.
- **Independent scaling.** Add workers when the queue grows, without touching the web servers.
- **Retries.** A message that fails can be tried again later.

The price is that the work is no longer finished when the user is told "done". The design has to make that honest: "your order is confirmed, an email is on its way".

steps.title: Delivery guarantees
steps.text:
A queue has to deal with a worker that crashes halfway through a message. There are two possible promises.

**At most once.** The message is removed from the queue when it is handed to a worker. If the worker crashes, the message is gone. Nothing is ever done twice, and some things are never done.

**At least once.** The message stays until the worker confirms that it finished. This confirmation is called an **acknowledgement**. If none arrives within a time limit, the queue hands the message to another worker. Nothing is lost, and some messages are processed twice. That happens whenever a worker finishes the work and crashes before it acknowledges.

Nearly all systems choose at least once, because losing work is usually worse than repeating it.

"Exactly once" is what everyone wants. In general it cannot be had from delivery alone. It is built from at-least-once delivery plus workers that can tolerate repeats.

steps.title: Make the worker safe to repeat
steps.text:
Since a message can arrive twice, a worker must be **idempotent**: handling the same message twice has the same effect as handling it once.

- **Use an ID.** Give every message a unique ID. Before doing the work, the worker checks whether that ID is already recorded as done. It records the ID in the same transaction as the work.
- **Write results that are naturally repeatable.** "Set the order's status to shipped" can be repeated. "Add 1 to the shipped count" cannot.
- **Pass the ID on.** When the work calls another service, such as a payment provider, send the message ID as the idempotency key, so that service can ignore repeats too.

steps.title: The repeated message
steps.text: A worker handles "add 50 loyalty points to customer 17" by running `points = points + 50`. Delivery is at least once. The worker crashes after the update and before the acknowledgement.

steps.title: Messages that never succeed
steps.text:
Some messages fail every time: the data is malformed, or it refers to a record that no longer exists. With unlimited retries, such a message is tried for ever. It is called a **poison message**.

The standard answer is a retry limit and a **dead-letter queue**. After a set number of failed attempts, such as five, the message is moved to a separate queue. There it stops blocking the others, and a person can inspect it.

A dead-letter queue needs an alert. Messages collecting there unseen are lost work that nobody knows about.

Retries should wait between attempts, with backoff. A message that failed because a dependency is down will fail again one millisecond later.

steps.title: Order is not guaranteed by default
steps.text:
With several workers, messages are finished in an unpredictable order. Worker A may take message 1 and be slow, while worker B takes message 2 and finishes first. Retries shuffle the order further.

Usually this does not matter. Where it does, as with "create account" before "update account", there are two approaches.

- **Order per key.** Many queue systems can keep order for messages that share a key, such as the account ID, while still handling different keys side by side.
- **Design for any order.** Put a version or a timestamp in each message, and have the worker ignore one that is older than what it has already applied.

Strict order across everything means one worker at a time, which gives up most of the benefit of a queue.

steps.title: When the queue keeps growing
steps.text:
A queue absorbs a burst. It cannot absorb a permanent gap. If messages arrive faster than the workers finish them hour after hour, the queue grows without end, the delay grows with it, and in time something runs out of space.

Two measures tell you the state of a queue: its **length**, and the **age of the oldest message**. A rising age means the workers are falling behind.

When that happens, the choices are:

- **Add workers**, if whatever they call can take the extra load.
- **Slow the producers.** Signalling "slow down" back up the chain is called **backpressure**. It can mean refusing new work with a clear error.
- **Drop or defer** work that has lost its value, such as a notification that is now an hour late.

A queue with no size limit hides an overload until it becomes a crisis. Give queues a limit and decide in advance what happens when it is reached.

steps.title: Scheduled and long-running work
steps.text:
The same pattern covers work that takes minutes, such as building an export or processing a video. The request creates a job record with the status "queued" and returns its ID at once. A worker does the job and updates the status. The client asks for the status from time to time, or is notified at the end.

This keeps long work out of request time limits, lets it survive a restart, and gives the user something to look at while they wait.

steps.title: Falling behind
steps.text: A queue receives 500 messages per second during the day. Its workers finish 400 per second in total. This goes on for one hour.

steps.title: Exercise: move work to a queue
steps.text:
A photo-sharing app handles an upload in one request. It saves the original file, creates three resized versions, scans the image for prohibited content, updates the user's storage total, and sends a push notification to the user's followers. The request takes 9 seconds and fails whenever the notification service is slow.

Decide what stays in the request and what moves to a queue. For each queued step, say how it is made safe to repeat and what the user sees while it is pending.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**In the request**

- Save the original file to object storage.
- Create the photo record with the status "processing".
- Put one message on the queue with the photo ID, and respond.

The request now takes well under a second and depends on nothing optional.

**On the queue**

| Step | Safe to repeat because | The user sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resize | The output files have fixed names derived from the photo ID. A repeat overwrites them with the same result. | A placeholder, then the photo |
| Content scan | It sets a status on the photo. Setting it twice is harmless. | "Processing" until it passes |
| Storage total | Recompute it from the user's files, or record the photo ID as counted. Never plain `total + size`. | A total that updates after a moment |
| Notification | Record "notified" per photo ID, and pass the photo ID to the push service as a key. | Nothing |

**Order.** The photo must not be shown to followers before the scan passes. So the scan sets the status to "visible", and only then is the notification message produced. Steps that depend on each other are chained, each producing the next message when it succeeds.

**Failure.** Each step retries with backoff, five times, and then goes to a dead-letter queue with an alert. A photo stuck in "processing" for more than a few minutes should be shown as failed with a way to try again.

choices.text: 100 points
