lessons.title: Events and streams
lessons.intro: A queue hands one piece of work to one worker. An event tells any number of interested parts that something happened. This module covers the difference, how an event log works, and what you take on when services communicate this way.

steps.title: Commands and events
steps.text:
Two kinds of message look alike and mean different things.

A **command** asks for something to be done: "send this email". It has one intended receiver, and the sender cares that it happens.

An **event** states that something has happened: "order 8841 was placed". It is a fact about the past. The sender does not know or care who reads it. Zero, one or ten parts of the system may react.

The difference decides who depends on whom. With commands, the order service must know about the email service, the warehouse service and the analytics service, and must change whenever one is added. With events, the order service announces "order placed" and knows nothing more. A new consumer is added without touching it.

steps.title: Publish and subscribe
steps.text:
The mechanism behind events is **publish/subscribe**. A producer publishes messages to a named **topic**. Each consumer **subscribes** to the topics it cares about, and every subscriber receives its own copy of every message.

Compare this with a work queue, where each message goes to exactly one worker.

| | Work queue | Publish/subscribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A message is handled by | One worker | Every subscriber |
| Adding a consumer | Shares the work | Adds a new reaction |
| Typical use | Spread jobs across workers | Tell several systems about a fact |

Both are often combined. Each subscriber gets its own queue of the events, and may run several workers on that queue.

steps.title: The log
steps.text:
Many event systems, with Apache Kafka as the best-known example, store events in a **log**: an ordered list that is only ever added to. Each event gets the next number in the list, called its **offset**.

A log differs from a queue in one important way. Reading an event does not remove it. Events stay for a set time, such as seven days, or for ever. Each consumer keeps its own position, which is the offset it has processed up to.

That gives the log three useful properties.

- **Many independent readers.** Each has its own position. A slow one does not hold up the others.
- **Replay.** A consumer can move its position back and read old events again. A new consumer can start from the beginning and build its own view of all past events. A consumer that had a bug can be fixed and run again over the same events.
- **Order.** Events are read in the order they were written.

steps.title: Order and partitions of a log
steps.text:
One log on one machine has a single order and a limit on how much it can take. To scale, a topic is split into several partitions, each its own log. Order is guaranteed inside a partition and not between partitions.

The producer chooses the partition by a key, the same idea as in the partitioning module. All events with the same key go to the same partition and therefore stay in order.

Choose the key by asking which events must stay in order relative to each other. For orders it is the order ID: "placed", "paid" and "shipped" for one order must be read in that sequence. Events of different orders can be handled in any order.

steps.title: Which order is kept
steps.text: A topic has 4 partitions, and events are placed by customer ID. Customer 17 produces "address changed" and then "order placed". Customer 42 produces "order placed" between those two.

steps.title: What an event should contain
steps.text:
There are two styles.

A **thin event** carries only identifiers: "order 8841 placed". A consumer that needs details calls the order service. The event stays small, and consumers always get current data. The cost is that every consumer calls back, so the load and the dependency return.

A **fat event** carries the data: the order with its lines, totals and address. Consumers need no call back and can work when the order service is down. The cost is larger messages, and the fact that the data is a snapshot of one moment.

Whichever you choose, an event is a public contract. Other teams' code depends on its fields. Treat changes as you would changes to an API: add fields freely, and never remove or rename one without a version and a migration plan.

steps.title: Writing to the database and publishing
steps.text:
A service often has to do two things for one action: save a change to its database and publish an event about it. These are two systems, and no transaction covers both.

- Save first, then publish: a crash in between leaves a saved order that nobody was told about.
- Publish first, then save: a crash in between announces an order that does not exist.

The standard solution is the **outbox pattern**. In the same database transaction that saves the order, the service also inserts a row into an "outbox" table that describes the event. A separate process reads the outbox and publishes each row, marking it as sent. If that process crashes, it starts again and may publish a row twice. So events are delivered at least once, and consumers must be idempotent, as in the queues module.

steps.title: The cost of events
steps.text:
Events loosen the ties between services, and they bring costs that are easy to miss at the start.

- **Everything is eventually consistent.** After "order placed", the warehouse's view is behind for a moment. Screens and processes must tolerate that.
- **The flow is hard to see.** With direct calls you can read the code and follow a request. With events, what happens after "order placed" is spread across every subscriber. Finding out why something did not happen takes good tracing and logs.
- **Failures are quiet.** A direct call that fails returns an error to someone. A consumer that silently stops is noticed only when its backlog is monitored.
- **Duplicates and reordering** have to be handled in every consumer.

Use events where several independent parts need to react to the same fact and none of them has to finish before the user gets an answer. Use a direct call when the caller needs the result to continue.

steps.title: Call or event
steps.text: At checkout, the order service must know whether the payment succeeded before it tells the user "order confirmed".

steps.title: Exercise: design the events
steps.text:
A library system lets members borrow and return books. When a book is returned, these things should happen: the book becomes available in the catalogue, the next person on the waiting list is notified, a late fee is charged if the book is overdue, and monthly statistics are updated.

Today the "return" endpoint calls four services one after another, and a failure in any of them fails the return. Redesign it with events. Name the event and its contents, say what stays in the request, and describe how each consumer copes with a duplicate.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**In the request.** The loans service marks the loan as returned and inserts a `book_returned` row in its outbox, in one transaction. It responds at once. The member sees "returned" as soon as the fact is recorded, whatever happens to the other services.

**The event.** `book_returned`, keyed by book ID so events for one copy stay in order. A fat event suits it: event ID, loan ID, book ID, member ID, due date and return time. No consumer needs to call back.

**Consumers**

| Consumer | Does | Copes with a duplicate by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalogue | Sets the copy to "available" | Setting a status twice changes nothing |
| Waiting list | Notifies the next member and holds the copy for them | Recording the event ID. A hold for this copy already exists |
| Fees | Charges a fee if the return time is after the due date | Recording the loan ID as charged, in the same transaction as the fee |
| Statistics | Adds to monthly counts | Recording processed event IDs, or recounting from stored events |

**What this changes.** A fault in the statistics service no longer stops a member from returning a book. A new reaction, such as "suggest similar books", is a new subscriber and needs no change to the loans service.

**What to watch.** The catalogue is now briefly behind: a returned book shows as "on loan" for a moment. And each consumer's backlog needs an alert, since a fee service that has stopped produces no error anywhere.

choices.text: All three events are read in the order they were produced
choices.feedback: Order across different partitions is not guaranteed.

choices.text: Customer 17's two events are read in order. Customer 42's event may come before, between or after them
choices.feedback: The same key means the same partition, which is ordered. Another key may be on another partition.

choices.text: No order at all
choices.feedback: Order inside one partition is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: How should the order service talk to the payment service at this point?

choices.text: With a direct call, and wait for the result
choices.feedback: The answer decides what the user is told. An event would leave the order service waiting for a reply event, which is a slower and more fragile way to make a call.

choices.text: By publishing "payment requested" and responding to the user at once

lessons.title: Design for failure
lessons.intro: In a system with many parts, something is broken most of the time. This module covers how failures spread, the patterns that stop them from spreading, and how to keep serving users when a part is down.

steps.title: Failure is the normal state
steps.text:
A single machine fails rarely, perhaps once every few years. A system of 1,000 machines therefore sees a failure most days. Add network faults, full disks, bad deploys, expired certificates and slow dependencies, and something is always wrong somewhere.

So the question for a design is not how to avoid failure. It is what happens when each part fails. Go through the drawing one box and one arrow at a time and ask:

- What does the user see if this stops?
- What does this part do if the thing it calls is slow?
- Does the failure stay here, or does it spread?

A design is good when the answers are "a small feature is missing" and "it stays here".

steps.title: Slow is worse than down
steps.text:
A dependency that is down fails fast. The caller gets an error in milliseconds and moves on.

A dependency that is slow is far more dangerous. Each call to it holds a thread, a connection and memory in the caller while it waits. As waiting calls pile up, the caller runs out of those resources and can no longer serve anything, including requests that never touch the slow dependency. Now the caller is slow, its own callers start piling up, and the failure climbs up the chain.

This is a **cascading failure**: one slow part takes down parts that were healthy.

steps.title: Timeouts, again
steps.text:
The first defence is the one from the networking course: every call has a timeout, and it is short. A timeout turns "slow" back into "failed fast", which the caller can handle.

Set it from the measured normal time, not from a guess. If a call normally takes 50 ms, a 30-second timeout offers no protection. A limit of a few hundred milliseconds does.

Retries need the same care as before: only for idempotent operations, with backoff and jitter, a small maximum, and at one layer only. A retry storm is the standard way a small failure becomes a large one.

steps.title: Circuit breakers
steps.text:
When a dependency keeps failing, even a short timeout on every call adds up. A **circuit breaker** stops the calls. It has three states.

- **Closed.** Calls pass through. The breaker counts failures.
- **Open.** After too many failures, calls fail at once without being sent. The dependency gets rest, and the caller wastes no time.
- **Half-open.** After a pause, a few test calls are let through. If they succeed, the breaker closes. If they fail, it opens again.

steps.title: Bulkheads
steps.text:
A ship's hull is divided into sealed compartments, so one leak floods one section and not the whole ship. A **bulkhead** in software does the same thing with resources.

Do not let all work share one pool. Give each dependency its own limited pool of connections or threads. If the recommendation service hangs, it can use up its own 20 connections and no more. The other 180 remain for everything else.

The same idea applies at larger scales: separate worker groups for slow reports and fast lookups, separate copies for a large customer, separate clusters per region.

steps.title: Where the limit helps
steps.text: A service has 200 worker threads. It calls a payment service and a recommendation service. Calls to recommendations start taking 60 seconds, with no timeout and no separate pools.

steps.title: Degrade, do not die
steps.text:
Most pages are built from several parts, and only some are essential. A product page needs the product and the price. Reviews, recommendations and "recently viewed" are extras.

**Graceful degradation** means serving the essential part when an extra fails. Each optional call gets a **fallback**: what to use in its place.

| Optional part | Fallback |
| --- | --- |
| Recommendations | Leave the section out, or show a fixed list of popular items |
| Review count | Show the last cached value, or nothing |
| Personalised greeting | Show a generic one |
| Search suggestions | Let the user type without them |

To design this, sort every dependency into required or optional. Be strict about the first group. Each required dependency is one more thing whose failure takes the feature down. A feature with five required dependencies that each work 99.9% of the time works only 99.5% of the time.

steps.title: Redundancy
steps.text:
A **single point of failure** is any one thing whose failure stops the system: one server, one database, one load balancer, one network link, one data centre. It can also be one person who knows how something works.

The remedy is **redundancy**: more than one of each, set up so the others take over.

- Several application copies behind a load balancer.
- A database leader with a follower that can be promoted.
- Copies spread across independent locations, called zones.

Redundancy helps only if the copies fail independently. Two servers in the same rack share a power supply. Two copies running the same faulty release fail together. A bad configuration pushed to all copies at once is the classic way a redundant system goes down entirely.

That is why changes are rolled out gradually: to one copy or a small share of traffic first, with a check before going further.

steps.title: Failing well at the edges
steps.text:
Three smaller habits make failures cheaper.

- **Fail fast.** Check inputs and required conditions at the start of a request. Rejecting a bad request after 5 seconds of work wastes the work.
- **Shed load.** A server that is over capacity should refuse some requests quickly with a `503`, not accept all of them and serve none. Serving 80% well beats serving 100% badly.
- **Make start-up independent.** A service that cannot start unless every dependency is up cannot be restarted during an outage, which is when restarts are needed most.

steps.title: Test the failure
steps.text:
A fallback that has never run probably does not work. Failure paths are the least exercised code in any system, and they are needed at the worst moment.

So failures are caused on purpose, under control: stop a copy, block a dependency, add delay to a call, fail over the database. Doing this as a regular practice is called **chaos engineering**. Start in a test environment and with small experiments, and state beforehand what you expect to happen.

A failover that is exercised every month is one you can trust. One that was set up two years ago and never tried is a guess.

steps.title: Which is required
steps.text: A checkout page calls four services: cart, payment, a fraud check, and a "customers also bought" service. Each is available 99.9% of the time, and all four are treated as required.

steps.title: Exercise: find the failure paths
steps.text:
A food delivery app's "place order" request does this, in order, with direct calls and no timeouts:

1. Reads the cart from a cache.
2. Calls the restaurant service to check that it is open.
3. Calls the payment service to charge the card.
4. Saves the order to the database.
5. Calls the notification service to alert the restaurant.
6. Calls a loyalty service to add points.
7. Calls an analytics service to record the sale.

For each step, say whether it is required for the order to be placed, what happens today if it is slow, and what you would change. Point out the step where a failure is most dangerous.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
| Step | Required? | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Cart from cache | Yes | Short timeout. Fall back to the database copy of the cart |
| 2. Restaurant open | Yes | Timeout of a few hundred ms. Circuit breaker. A cached "open" status may be good enough |
| 3. Payment | Yes | Timeout. Idempotency key, so a retry cannot charge twice |
| 4. Save order | Yes | Must succeed, see below |
| 5. Notify restaurant | Yes, soon after | Queue it, with retries and an alert if it is not delivered within a minute |
| 6. Loyalty points | No | Event or queue |
| 7. Analytics | No | Event or queue |

**Today.** With no timeouts, a slow analytics service holds every order request open. Orders stop because a reporting system is slow, which is the cascade described earlier.

**The dangerous step.** Between 3 and 4. If the payment succeeds and the save then fails, the customer has paid for an order that does not exist. Reverse the order of work: save the order as "pending payment" first, then charge with the order ID as the idempotency key, then mark it "paid". A crash at any point now leaves a record that a background job can finish or refund.

**After the change.** The request needs only the cache or database, the restaurant check and the payment. Steps 5 to 7 react to an "order placed" event. Step 5 differs from 6 and 7: it is not needed for the response, and it is essential to the business, so it needs its own alert when it falls behind.

lessons.title: Availability and recovery
lessons.intro: "The system must always be up" is not a requirement anyone can build to. This module covers how availability is measured, how the parts of a system combine, and how to plan for the day when a whole site is lost.

steps.title: Measuring availability
steps.text:
**Availability** is the share of time, or of requests, in which the system works. It is written as a percentage and often spoken of in "nines".

| Availability | Downtime per year | Downtime per month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 99% (two nines) | 3.7 days | 7.3 hours |
| 99.9% (three nines) | 8.8 hours | 44 minutes |
| 99.99% (four nines) | 53 minutes | 4.4 minutes |
| 99.999% (five nines) | 5.3 minutes | 26 seconds |

Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by ten and costs far more than the one before. At 99.9% a person can be woken up and fix things by hand. At 99.99% there are four minutes a month, so every recovery must be automatic. At 99.999% even a deploy has to be invisible.

So choose the target from what downtime costs the business, and do not reach for the highest number. An internal tool used in office hours has no need for four nines.

steps.title: Parts in a row and parts side by side
steps.text:
The availability of a system follows from its parts in two ways.

**In a row (all needed).** If a request needs A and B and C, multiply. Three parts at 99.9% each give 99.7%. Every required part lowers the total.

**Side by side (any one is enough).** If either of two copies can do the job, the system fails only when both fail together. Two copies at 99% each give 99.99%, provided they fail independently.

This gives the two rules of available design: have as few required parts as possible, and have more than one of each.

steps.title: What the numbers say
steps.text: A service is deployed as a single copy that is available 99.5% of the time. It depends on one database at 99.9% and on an external provider at 99.5%. All three are required.

steps.title: SLI, SLO and SLA
steps.text:
Three terms make a target precise.

- An **SLI** (service level indicator) is a measurement: "the share of requests answered successfully in under 500 ms".
- An **SLO** (service level objective) is the target for it: "99.9% over 30 days".
- An **SLA** (service level agreement) is a contract with customers that says what happens if a level is missed, such as a refund. It is set lower than the internal SLO, to leave a margin.

Measure what the user experiences. "The server process is running" is a poor indicator. A server can be running and return errors, or be so slow that nobody waits. Count requests that succeeded and were fast enough, measured as close to the user as you can.

steps.title: The error budget
steps.text:
An SLO of 99.9% allows 0.1% of requests to fail. That allowance is the **error budget**. In a month of 10 million requests it is 10,000 failures.

The budget turns reliability into something a team can decide with.

- While budget remains, the team can release changes quickly and take risks.
- When the budget is spent, releases slow down and the effort goes to reliability until the service is back within its target.

It also settles the argument about whether to aim for 100%. A system with no budget for failure can never be changed, since every change carries some risk.

steps.title: Kinds of redundancy
steps.text:
A standby can be kept in different states of readiness. The more ready it is, the more it costs and the faster it takes over.

| Kind | The spare is | Takeover takes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cold | Switched off, or exists only as a backup | Hours |
| Warm | Running at small size, data kept up to date | Minutes |
| Hot (active-passive) | Running at full size, takes no traffic | Seconds to a minute |
| Active-active | Running and serving traffic already | Nearly no time. The others just carry more |

Active-active looks like the obvious choice, and it has two costs. Each site must have room to carry the load of one that fails. And the data must be writable in more than one place, which brings the conflicts from the consistency module.

steps.title: Zones and regions
steps.text:
Cloud providers offer two levels of separation.

A **zone** is one or more data centres with their own power and network. Zones in the same region are a few milliseconds apart. Spreading copies over three zones protects against the loss of a building, and the short distance means a database can replicate synchronously between them. This is the normal design and should be the default.

A **region** is a set of zones in one part of the world. Regions are tens or hundreds of milliseconds apart. Running in two regions protects against the loss of a whole region and puts the service near more users. The distance makes synchronous replication slow, so the design must accept either slower writes or some lost data on failover.

Most systems should be multi-zone. Multi-region is a large step in cost and complexity. Take it when a requirement names it: a regional outage is unacceptable, or users far away need low latency.

steps.title: Disaster recovery: RPO and RTO
steps.text:
Some events are larger than a failed machine: a region goes down, data is corrupted by a bug, an account is compromised. Planning for these is **disaster recovery**. Two numbers define the goal.

- **RPO** (recovery point objective): how much data may be lost, measured as time. An RPO of 5 minutes means that after recovery, at most the last 5 minutes of changes are gone.
- **RTO** (recovery time objective): how long recovery may take. An RTO of 1 hour means service is restored within an hour.

They are set by the business and they decide the method.

| Method | RPO | RTO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nightly backups, restored by hand | up to 24 hours | hours to a day |
| Backups plus a continuous change log | minutes | hours |
| A warm standby in another region, asynchronous | seconds | minutes |
| Active-active in two regions | close to zero | close to zero |

steps.title: A plan that was never tried
steps.text:
A recovery plan has value only if it works, and the only way to know is to run it.

- **Restore a backup** on a schedule, into a test environment, and check the data.
- **Fail over** on purpose, in a planned window, and measure how long it really takes.
- **Write the steps down** as a runbook: an ordered list that a person who is tired and under pressure can follow.
- **Check the dependencies of the recovery itself.** If the runbook, the passwords or the deploy tool live only in the region that failed, there is no plan.

Teams that practise recovery find the gaps on a quiet afternoon. Teams that do not find them during the outage.

steps.title: Which target fits
steps.text: A payroll system runs a pay calculation once a month. Staff use it on working days. Losing a day of entered data would mean re-entering it by hand, which is annoying and possible.

steps.title: Exercise: set the targets
steps.text:
A hospital runs an appointment booking system. Patients book online at any hour. Reception staff use it from 07:00 to 19:00. If it is down, staff fall back to paper for a short time. A lost booking means a patient who arrives and is not expected.

Propose an SLI, an SLO, an RPO and an RTO, each with a reason. Then describe the redundancy you would use, and name two things you would test regularly.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**SLI.** The share of booking and schedule requests that succeed in under 1 second, measured at the load balancer.

**SLO.** 99.9% over 30 days, which allows about 44 minutes a month. Paper covers short gaps, and four nines would cost a great deal more for little gain. It may be worth a separate, stricter target for 07:00 to 19:00, when a failure hits staff and patients together.

**RPO.** Zero for confirmed bookings. A lost booking has a real cost to a patient. That means a confirmed write must be on two machines before it is acknowledged.

**RTO.** 15 minutes. Paper works for that long without real harm.

**Redundancy**

- Application copies in three zones behind a load balancer, with room to lose one zone.
- A database leader with a synchronous follower in a second zone and an asynchronous one in a third. Failover is automatic.
- Backups with a continuous change log, stored in a second region. They protect against a regional loss and against mistakes, with an RPO of minutes and an RTO of hours for that rare case.

A second live region is not justified by these requirements. Stating that as a decision is part of the design.

**Test regularly**

1. Restore a backup into a test environment every month and check that recent bookings are there.
2. Fail the database over to the follower every quarter, during a quiet period, and measure the time against the 15-minute RTO.

lessons.title: See what the system is doing
lessons.intro: A system you cannot see into can only be fixed by guessing. This module covers the three kinds of signal a system gives off, what to measure, and how to alert on the things that matter without waking people for the things that do not.

steps.title: Three kinds of signal
steps.text:
A running system should tell you what it is doing in three ways. Each answers a different question.

| Signal | What it is | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Metrics** | Numbers measured over time | Is something wrong, and since when? |
| **Logs** | Records of single events | What exactly happened to this request? |
| **Traces** | The path of one request through every service | Where did the time go, and which service failed? |

They are used in that order. A metric shows that the error rate rose at 14:02. A trace of one failing request shows that the time was lost in the payment service. The logs of that service show the error message.

The ability to answer new questions about a system from its signals, without changing its code, is called **observability**.

steps.title: Metrics
steps.text:
A **metric** is a number sampled at regular intervals and stored with a timestamp: requests per second, error rate, queue length, memory in use. Metrics are cheap to keep, since they are totals and not one record per request, and they can be drawn as graphs.

For any service that answers requests, four measurements tell you most of what you need. They are often called the **four golden signals**.

- **Traffic.** How much is being asked: requests per second.
- **Errors.** The share of requests that fail.
- **Latency.** How long requests take, as percentiles.
- **Saturation.** How full the service is: processor, memory, connections, queue length.

The first three describe what users experience. The fourth warns you before they experience anything.

steps.title: Percentiles, not averages
steps.text:
Latency must be recorded as **percentiles**. The p50 is the time that half of the requests beat. The p99 is the time that 99 out of 100 beat.

An average hides the slow requests. If 99 requests take 100 ms and one takes 10 seconds, the average is 199 ms, which describes no request at all. The p99 of 10 seconds describes the one user in a hundred who had a bad time.

At scale that one percent is many people. With 1,000 requests per second, a bad p99 means 10 slow requests every second.

steps.title: Logs
steps.text:
A **log** line records one event: a request handled, an error, a decision the code made. Logs carry the detail that metrics leave out.

Two practices make logs useful at scale.

**Structured logs.** Write each entry as fields, usually JSON, and not as a free sentence. A field can be searched and counted. A sentence has to be picked apart by pattern.

**A request ID on every line.** Create an ID when a request enters the system, pass it to every service it touches, and include it in every log line. Then one search gathers everything that happened to that request, across all services. It is also called a correlation ID.


Two cautions. Logs are costly in volume, so choose levels with care and sample the routine ones. And logs must not contain secrets or personal data: no passwords, tokens, card numbers or full request bodies. That last point is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

steps.title: Traces
steps.text:
A **trace** follows one request through every service it passes. It is made of **spans**. A span is one piece of work, with a start time, a duration and the ID of the span that caused it.

Drawn on a time axis, a trace shows at a glance where the time went and which calls ran side by side or one after another.

steps.title: What does it show
steps.text: A page is slow. Its trace shows 30 spans to the same database, each 8 ms, one after another, and nothing else of note.

steps.title: Alert on what users feel
steps.text:
An **alert** asks a person to act. A good alert is urgent, about something real, and something that person can do something about. Most bad alerting comes from breaking one of those three.

The most useful rule is to alert on **symptoms**, not causes. A symptom is something a user experiences: errors, slowness, wrong results. A cause is something inside the system: high processor use, a restarted process, a full disk.

- Processor use at 90% may be perfectly fine if requests are fast and succeeding.
- A process that restarts and recovers by itself needs no human.
- An error rate above the SLO always matters, whatever caused it.

Alert on the symptom and use the cause metrics on a dashboard to find the reason. The exceptions are causes that will certainly become symptoms and give you time to act: a disk that will be full in four hours, a certificate that expires in two weeks.

| Alert | Good? |
| --- | --- |
| Error rate above 1% for 5 minutes | Yes. Users are affected |
| p99 latency above the SLO for 10 minutes | Yes |
| Disk will be full within 4 hours | Yes. It is certain, and there is time to act |
| Processor use above 80% | No. Not a problem by itself |
| One request failed | No. A single failure is noise |

steps.title: Alert fatigue
steps.text:
Every alert that turns out not to matter teaches people to ignore alerts. After enough of them, the real one is missed. This is **alert fatigue**, and it is how monitored systems still have long outages.

Treat a noisy alert as a bug. For each one that fires, ask: did someone need to act? If not, fix the alert: raise its threshold, require it to last longer, or delete it. Separate two levels clearly. A **page** wakes someone now. A **ticket** waits for working hours.

Every alert should link to a short runbook: what it means, what to check first, and how to make things better for now.

steps.title: Dashboards
steps.text:
A dashboard for a service should answer one question in ten seconds: is it healthy? Put the four golden signals at the top. Mark deploys and configuration changes on the time axis, since most incidents begin with a change. Put the detail below for when the top shows a problem.

A dashboard with a hundred graphs answers no question. Fewer graphs, each chosen for a reason, serve better.

steps.title: Monitor from outside too
steps.text:
Everything above is measured inside the system. If the load balancer is down, or DNS is wrong, no request arrives, so the inside sees no errors at all. The graphs look calm while every user is locked out.

A **synthetic check** closes that gap. A small program outside your network performs a real user action every minute, such as loading the login page, and alerts when it fails. It is the only signal that covers the whole path, including the parts you do not run.

steps.title: The quiet outage
steps.text: At 03:00 a DNS record is deleted by mistake. The site becomes unreachable. The service's dashboard shows an error rate of 0% and no latency problems.

steps.title: Exercise: instrument a service
steps.text:
A checkout service receives requests from a web front end, calls a payment provider and a stock service, and writes orders to a database. It currently logs free-text lines and has no metrics or traces. Last week it was slow for two hours before anyone noticed.

List the metrics you would add, what each log line must contain, what tracing needs, and the three alerts you would create. Say which single addition would have shortened last week's two hours the most.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Metrics**

- Requests per second, by endpoint.
- Error rate, by endpoint and by status code.
- Latency as p50, p95 and p99, by endpoint.
- The same three for each outbound call: payment, stock and database.
- Saturation: processor, memory, the connection pool in use, and the length of any queue.

Measuring each dependency separately is what tells you whose fault a slowdown is.

**Logs.** Structured, with the time, level, service, request ID, endpoint, status and duration. No card data and no tokens.

**Tracing.** Create a request ID at the front end, pass it in a header through every call, and record one span for each outbound call.

**Alerts**

1. Page: checkout error rate above 1% for 5 minutes.
2. Page: checkout p99 latency above 2 seconds for 10 minutes.
3. Page: a synthetic check that performs a test checkout every minute fails three times in a row.

A ticket-level alert on connection pool use above 80% gives early warning without waking anyone.

**What would have helped most.** The latency alert. The slowness lasted two hours because nobody was told. The traces and per-dependency metrics would then have shortened the search for the cause. Noticing comes first, and noticing is what an alert is for.

questions.prompt: What is the cause?

choices.text: The database is slow

choices.text: The network between the services is slow
choices.feedback: A slow network would stretch each span. Each one is short. There are simply too many.

questions.prompt: Why does the dashboard look healthy, and what would have caught it?

choices.text: The dashboard is broken
choices.feedback: It is working. It reports what the servers see.

choices.text: No requests reach the servers, so there is nothing to fail. A check from outside, or an alert on traffic dropping to zero, would have caught it
choices.feedback: Error rate is failures divided by requests. With no requests it stays at zero. The outage is visible only from the user's side, or as missing traffic.

choices.text: DNS failures never last long enough to matter
choices.feedback: A deleted record stays deleted until somebody restores it.

lessons.title: Protect the system from overload
lessons.intro: Every system has a limit. What matters is how it behaves when more work arrives than it can do. This module covers what overload looks like, and the tools for refusing work early so that the work you accept still gets done.

steps.title: What happens past the limit
steps.text:
Below its limit, a server finishes work as fast as it arrives. Past the limit you might expect it to keep working at full capacity and leave the extra waiting. In practice, an unprotected system does much worse than that.

- Requests queue up, so each one waits longer.
- Clients time out and give up, and the server still does the work for an answer nobody will read.
- Clients retry, which adds load.
- Memory fills with waiting requests, and the process slows down or crashes.

The useful output can fall close to zero while the server is busier than ever. This is **congestion collapse**. A system that could serve 1,000 requests per second serves almost none when offered 1,500.

The goal of everything in this module is to make the curve flat: at 1,500 offered, serve 1,000 well and refuse 500 quickly.

steps.title: Rate limiting
steps.text:
A **rate limit** caps how many requests one client may make in a period: 100 per minute per API key, 5 login attempts per minute per account. A request over the limit gets `429 Too Many Requests` at once, with a `Retry-After` header that says when to try again.

Rate limits protect against one client using up capacity that everyone shares, whether through a bug, a runaway script or an attack. They also keep usage fair.

The most common method is the **token bucket**.

- Each client has a bucket that holds a maximum number of tokens.
- Tokens are added at a steady rate, up to the maximum.
- Each request takes one token. With no token left, the request is refused.

The refill rate sets the long-run average. The bucket size sets how large a short burst may be. A client that has been quiet has a full bucket and can send a burst. A client that sends constantly is held to the refill rate.

steps.title: Where to count
steps.text:
Two decisions shape a rate limit.

**What to count by.** By API key or user ID is the most accurate. By client address is the fallback for requests with no identity, and it is rough: many users behind one office share an address, and an attacker can use many. For logins, count by the account being tried as well as by address.

**Where to count.** With several application copies, a count kept in each copy's memory lets a client have the limit once per copy. The count belongs in a shared store, or at the gateway or load balancer in front of all the copies.

steps.title: The limit that was not
steps.text: A service limits each API key to 100 requests per minute. Each of its 8 copies keeps the count in its own memory. The load balancer spreads requests evenly.

steps.title: Load shedding
steps.text:
A rate limit acts on one client. **Load shedding** acts on the whole system. When the server is over capacity, it refuses some requests on purpose, quickly and with a `503`, so that the ones it accepts finish in good time.

It works because refusing is cheap. Rejecting a request at the door costs a fraction of a millisecond. Accepting it, queueing it for 20 seconds and timing out costs real resources and helps nobody.

How to decide when to shed:

- **A limit on requests in progress.** Accept at most N at once and refuse beyond that.
- **A limit on queue length or queue time.** If a request has already waited longer than its caller's timeout, drop it. The caller has gone.
- **By priority.** Refuse the least important work first.

steps.title: Not all requests are equal
steps.text:
When something must be refused, choose what. Sort requests into classes before the overload comes.

| Class | Examples | Under overload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Critical | Checkout, login, health checks | Refused last |
| Normal | Browsing, search | Shed when needed |
| Background | Reports, exports, recomputation | Shed first, or paused |

Two details matter. Health checks must keep answering, or the load balancer removes the overloaded copies and pushes their load onto the rest. And a user who is halfway through a checkout is worth more than a new visitor, so work already in progress is protected before new work.

steps.title: Backpressure
steps.text:
Shedding refuses work at the door. **Backpressure** tells the sender to slow down, so the work is not produced in the first place.

Inside a system it takes several forms.

- A bounded queue that makes the producer wait or fail when it is full.
- A worker that takes new work only when it has room.
- A `429` or `503` with `Retry-After`, which a well-behaved client obeys.

The alternative is an unbounded buffer somewhere in the chain. It accepts everything, grows quietly, and turns a brief overload into a long delay and then into a crash. Every queue and buffer in a design should have a size limit, and the design should say what happens when the limit is reached.

steps.title: Clients must cooperate
steps.text:
Protection on the server works far better when clients behave well. The rules are the ones from the networking course, seen from the other side.

- Honour `Retry-After`.
- Back off exponentially with jitter. Never retry at once in a loop.
- Limit retries, and retry only what is safe to repeat.
- Use a circuit breaker, so a failing service stops receiving calls.

If you write both the client and the server, build these in from the start. A million mobile apps that all retry every second can keep a recovering service down indefinitely.

steps.title: Planned surges
steps.text:
Some overloads are known in advance: a sale, a ticket release, a product launch. Three techniques shape such a surge.

- **Scale before the event.** Autoscaling reacts in minutes. Add the capacity an hour ahead.
- **A waiting room.** Admit users at a rate the system can serve, and show the rest their place in line. An honest queue is a far better experience than a page that fails.
- **Do less per request.** Turn off optional features for the duration: recommendations, live counts, anything not needed to complete the purchase.

steps.title: Which to refuse
steps.text: A service is at 130% of its capacity. In its queue are health checks from the load balancer, checkout requests, product page views and requests for a monthly report export.

steps.title: Exercise: design the protection
steps.text:
A public API for a mapping service has free and paid customers. Its 10 copies can serve 5,000 requests per second in total. Last month a free customer's script went into a loop and sent 4,000 requests per second for 20 minutes. Paid customers saw timeouts. There are no limits of any kind today.

Design the protection: rate limits, where they are counted, what is shed under overload and in which order, and what a refused client receives. Say what would have happened last month with your design.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Rate limits, per API key, as token buckets**

| Plan | Refill | Burst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | 10 per second | 50 |
| Paid | 200 per second | 1,000 |

They are counted at the API gateway in front of the copies, with the counters in a shared in-memory store, so the limit is the same however many copies run. Requests with no key are limited by address, strictly.

**Shedding.** Each copy accepts at most a fixed number of requests in progress and refuses beyond it. Under overload, shed in this order: free-plan requests, then batch endpoints for paid plans, then the rest. Health checks are never shed.

**What a refused client gets.** `429` with `Retry-After` for a rate limit. `503` with `Retry-After` for shedding. Both arrive in under a millisecond and are documented, with advice to back off with jitter.

**Capacity.** Alert when total traffic passes 70% of capacity, and autoscale on requests per copy.

**Last month, with this design.** The looping script would have had 50 requests answered and then received `429` for the other 3,990 or so each second. Refusing them costs almost nothing. Paid customers would have noticed nothing. The free customer would have seen a clear error that pointed to the bug in their script.

The 20-minute incident becomes a line in a log. That is the difference between a system with limits and one without.

choices.feedback: Each copy sees only an eighth of the client's requests.

choices.text: About 800
choices.feedback: Every copy allows 100 before it refuses. The real limit is the configured one multiplied by the number of copies, and it changes whenever copies are added.

choices.text: About 12
choices.feedback: That would be the result if the limit were divided among the copies. Each copy applies the full 100.

questions.prompt: What should it shed first?

choices.text: Health checks, since they do no useful work
choices.feedback: If health checks fail, the load balancer takes this copy out and sends its traffic to the others, which are overloaded too.

choices.text: The oldest requests, whatever they are
choices.feedback: Age matters once a request has outlived its caller's timeout. Before that, importance is the better guide.

choices.text: The report exports, then page views if needed
choices.feedback: Exports can run later with no harm. Checkout is the work the business exists for and is refused last.

lessons.title: Worked design: a link shortener
lessons.intro: This module walks through one complete design using the five steps from the first module. Nothing in it is new. The aim is to see the earlier ideas used together, in order, with each addition justified by a number.

steps.title: The request
steps.text:
"Design a service that turns a long web address into a short one. Opening the short one takes the visitor to the long one."

It sounds like a weekend project, and at a small size it is. It is used here because every design step shows up in a problem you can hold in your head.

Follow the five steps: requirements, numbers, interface and data, a simple design, then pressure.

steps.title: Step 1: requirements
steps.text:
**What it must do**

- Create a short link for a long address.
- Redirect anyone who opens the short link.
- Count how often each link is opened.

**Out of scope for now:** custom names, expiry dates, user accounts beyond an API key, and editing a link after it is made.

**How well**

| Question | Answer assumed |
| --- | --- |
| How many new links? | 10 million per month |
| How many opens? | 100 opens for every link created |
| How fast must a redirect be? | Under 100 ms for nearly all visitors |
| May a link ever stop working? | No. Links are kept for years |
| How fresh must the open count be? | A few minutes old is fine |
| What if the service is down? | Every link everywhere is dead, so redirects need high availability |

Two things stand out already. The system is very read-heavy. And the two operations differ in importance: a failed redirect breaks other people's pages, while a failed creation only annoys one person, who can try again.

steps.title: Step 2: numbers
steps.text:
Round hard, as in the estimates module.


These numbers are small. Twenty writes per second is nothing for a database. 300 GB after five years fits on one machine. Two thousand reads per second is within reach of a single database, though worth easing.

The estimate has already made a decision: this system does not need partitioning. It would have been easy to assume otherwise.

steps.title: Sizing check
steps.text: Based on the numbers above, which part of the design needs the most care?

steps.title: Step 3: interface and data
steps.text:
Two operations.


One table.

| Column | Type | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | text, primary key | The short code |
| `url` | text | The long address |
| `created_at` | timestamp | |
| `owner` | text | The API key that created it |

The only question the system asks at volume is "give me the row with this code". That is a lookup by one key, the simplest access pattern there is. A relational database serves it well, and so would a key-value store. A relational database is chosen here because it is the default and nothing argues against it.

A choice hides in the status code. `301` means moved for good, and browsers remember it and skip the service next time. That is fast, and those opens are never counted. `302` means temporary, so every open comes back to the service. Counting opens is a requirement, so the design uses `302`.

steps.title: How long is a code, and how is it made
steps.text:
A code uses 62 characters: a to z, A to Z and 0 to 9. Six characters give 62 to the power 6, about 57 billion codes. The system needs 600 million in five years, so six is plenty, with room to spare. Seven would give 3.5 trillion.

There are two ways to produce a code.

**From a counter.** Keep a number that goes up by one for each link, and write it in base 62. Codes never collide. They are also guessable: after `k3Xp9a` comes `k3Xp9b`, so anyone can walk through every link. A single counter is also one more thing shared between all copies.

**At random.** Pick six random characters and insert the row. The primary key refuses a duplicate, in which case pick again. With 600 million of 57 billion codes in use, about one attempt in a hundred collides, and a second try settles it. Codes cannot be guessed in sequence.

The design uses random codes. Links often point at things that are private by obscurity, and a retry on one write in a hundred, at 20 writes per second, is no cost at all.

steps.title: Step 4: the simple design
steps.text:
Two application copies, since one would be a single point of failure. They are stateless, so any copy answers any request.

Check it against the numbers. The peak of 2,000 reads per second by primary key is possible for one database and close to the range where it deserves help. Writes are trivial. Storage is fine.

Now check it against the requirements. Two are not met.

1. Redirects need high availability, and the single database is a single point of failure.
2. Open counts are not recorded anywhere yet.

Those two, and only those, drive step 5.

steps.title: Step 5: apply pressure
steps.text:
**Availability of redirects.** Add a database follower in a second zone, with automatic failover. A confirmed link must not be lost, so that follower is synchronous. Spread the application copies over the zones.

**Read load and speed.** Add a cache in front of the database. A link never changes after it is made, which makes it the ideal thing to cache: there is no invalidation problem. Use cache-aside with a long TTL. Popular links are opened again and again, so the hit rate will be high, and most redirects never reach the database.

That also helps availability. If the database is briefly unreachable, links that are in the cache still work.

**Counting opens.** Writing to the database on every redirect would turn 2,000 reads per second into 2,000 writes per second, on the path where speed matters most. The count may be a few minutes old, so take it off that path. On each redirect the application publishes a small "link opened" event and answers at once. A consumer adds the events up and writes totals to the database every minute.

If the event system is down, redirects must still work. So publishing is best effort: a failure to publish is logged and the redirect goes ahead. That is a stated trade-off. In a rare failure, some opens go uncounted.

steps.title: What was decided against
steps.text:
A design is also the list of things left out, with reasons.

- **No partitioning.** 300 GB in five years fits on one machine. Revisit at ten times the volume.
- **No second region.** Zones cover the availability requirement. Visitors far away pay one extra round trip of distance. If the latency requirement tightens, serve redirects from several regions with read-only copies of the data, which is easy here because links never change.
- **No strong consistency for counts.** They are eventual, and losing a few in a failure is accepted.
- **No protection designed yet.** A real service needs rate limits on creation per API key, and a check that refuses links to known harmful sites. Both sit at the front and change nothing behind it.

steps.title: The cached link
steps.text: A link is created and cached with a TTL of 24 hours. The requirements say links cannot be edited.

steps.title: Exercise: extend the design
steps.text:
The product team adds two requirements.

1. A link's owner can delete it. A deleted link must stop working within one minute.
2. Links can be given an expiry time, after which they stop working.

Say what changes in the data, in the cache and in the redirect path. Then say which earlier statement in this module is no longer true.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Data.** Add two columns: `deleted_at` and `expires_at`, both empty by default.

**Redirect path.** Fetch the row, or its cached copy. If it is deleted, or its expiry time has passed, answer `410 Gone`. That status tells the visitor the link existed and has been removed, which is more accurate than `404`.

**Expiry and the cache.** Store `expires_at` inside the cached value and compare it with the clock on every request. A cached copy then stays correct however long it is kept. No invalidation is needed for expiry.

**Deletion and the cache.** This is the real change. A deleted link may sit in the cache for up to 24 hours. Two measures together meet the one-minute rule.

- On delete, update the database and delete the cache entry, as in cache-aside.
- Lower the TTL to 60 seconds, as the safety net for a missed delete.

At 2,000 reads per second, a 60-second TTL still gives a hit rate well above 90% for popular links.

**What is no longer true.** "A link never changes after it is made, so there is no invalidation problem." That sentence carried the cache design. One small feature removed it. This is why a design should write its assumptions down: when a requirement changes, you can find every decision that rested on it.

questions.prompt: Where should the effort go?

choices.text: Storing the data, since links are kept for years
choices.feedback: 300 GB in five years fits on one ordinary database server.

choices.text: Handling the write load
choices.feedback: 20 writes per second at peak is far below what one database can take.

choices.text: Making redirects fast and always available
choices.feedback: Reads are 100 times the writes, every one has a visitor waiting, and an outage breaks every link at once.

questions.prompt: Why is this cache much simpler than the ones in the caching module?

choices.text: Because the TTL is long
choices.feedback: A long TTL on data that changes would make things worse, not simpler.

choices.text: Because the data never changes, so a cached copy can never be out of date
choices.feedback: There is no invalidation on write and no staleness to reason about. If editing or deleting links is added later, that changes, and the cache design must be revisited.

choices.text: Because links are small
choices.feedback: Size affects how many fit in memory. It has nothing to do with correctness.

lessons.title: Review a design and make one
lessons.intro: This module has no new ideas. You review a design with faults in it and then make a design of your own. Do each exercise on paper before you read its answer.

steps.title: How to use this module
steps.text:
Each exercise has a step where you work alone and a step with one possible answer. The answers are not the only good ones. Compare your reasoning with them, and pay most attention to anything you did not consider at all.

When you review a design, ask the same questions each time.

1. What are the numbers, and does each part fit them?
2. Where is the single point of failure?
3. What happens when each dependency is slow?
4. Which data can be stale, and which must not be?
5. Which part has no stated reason to exist?

The fifth question is as useful as the others. A design can be wrong by having too much in it.

steps.title: Review 1: an event ticket system
steps.text: A team presents this design for selling concert tickets. Sales open at a fixed time, and popular events sell out within minutes. Read it and list every problem you find. Rank them.

steps.title: The most urgent one
steps.text: Before you read the full list, choose from three of the faults.

steps.title: Review 1: what is wrong
steps.text:
**Correctness**

1. **Overselling.** "Read, then subtract" is not atomic. Make it one step in the database: decrease the count only if it is above zero, inside a transaction, and sell only when that succeeds.
2. **Seat counts in memory.** A crash loses up to 30 seconds of sales. Tickets that were sold become available again. The database must be the source of truth for every sale.
3. **Five immediate retries of a charge.** Without an idempotency key, a customer can be charged several times. With one, the retries still hit a struggling payment provider all at once. Send a key, back off, and limit the retries.

**Capacity**

4. **One server for 80,000 people at once.** The estimate takes one line: 80,000 arrivals in the first minute is over 1,300 requests per second before anyone refreshes. Run many stateless copies, scaled up before the sale starts.
5. **12 queries per event page.** The page is the same for every visitor. Cache it at the CDN for a few seconds, and nearly all of that load disappears.
6. **Logins in memory.** They prevent running more than one copy. Move them to a shared store.

**Failure**

7. **Email in the request, with no timeout.** A slow provider stops ticket sales. Queue the email and respond as soon as the sale is recorded.
8. **Single points of failure.** One server, one database. Add copies and a database follower with failover.
9. **Weekly backups.** Up to a week of sales could be lost. Keep the change log continuously, and test a restore.

**Missing altogether**

10. **Nothing for the surge.** Use a waiting room that admits buyers at the rate the purchase path can serve, and rate limits per account.
11. **No seat hold.** A buyer needs a short reservation, such as five minutes, while they pay. Otherwise the seat is sold to someone else during payment.

Items 1 to 3 come first because they produce wrong outcomes that involve money. The others produce a slow or unavailable system, which is bad and can be recovered from.

steps.title: Design: a notification service
steps.text:
Design a service that other teams call to notify users. A caller says "tell user 17 that their order shipped", and the service delivers it by push notification, email or SMS according to the user's settings.

Assume 5 million users, 20 million notifications a day, and bursts of 2 million within a few minutes when marketing sends a campaign. Order updates should arrive within about 10 seconds. Campaign messages may take up to an hour. A user must not receive the same notification twice. Each external provider (push, email, SMS) has its own rate limit and fails from time to time.

Work through the five steps. Write the requirements you would confirm, the numbers, the interface, a simple design, and what you add under pressure with the reason for each addition.

steps.title: Design: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Requirements to confirm.** Are there quiet hours? Can a user opt out per kind of message? Is delivery status needed by callers? This answer assumes yes to opt-out, and that status is stored for 30 days.

**Numbers.** 20 million a day is 200 per second on average. A campaign of 2 million in 5 minutes is about 7,000 per second. A status record of 300 bytes for 30 days is about 180 GB. So the average is modest, the burst is 35 times larger, and the burst is made of messages that may wait.

**Interface.** One call: `POST /notifications` with a user ID, a kind, the content, a priority and an idempotency key chosen by the caller. It answers `202 Accepted` with an ID. `202` is honest: the service accepted the work and has not done it yet.

**Simple design.** The API validates the request and writes it to a queue. Workers take a message, look up the user's settings, call the right provider and record the result. That is the whole shape, and each addition below has a reason.


**Under pressure**

| Addition | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Two queues, by priority | A campaign of 2 million must not delay an order update. With one queue, the 10-second target fails during every campaign |
| Idempotency key stored on acceptance | Callers retry, and the queue delivers at least once. The key is checked on acceptance and again before sending |
| A rate limit per provider, in the workers | Each provider has a limit. Going over it gets the service blocked |
| A circuit breaker and a separate worker pool per provider | A slow SMS provider must not stop push and email. This is a bulkhead |
| Retries with backoff, then a dead-letter queue with an alert | Providers fail briefly. A message that never succeeds must not block the others |
| A cache for user settings | Every message needs them, and they change rarely. Opt-outs must take effect fast, so delete the entry on change and use a short TTL |
| Autoscaling of workers on queue age | The load is bursty. The age of the oldest message is the signal that matters to users |
| A rate limit per caller on the API | One team's bug must not flood every user |

**The hard part: never twice.** At-least-once delivery, plus a worker that can crash between "provider accepted" and "recorded as sent", means a duplicate is possible. Pass the notification ID to the provider as its own idempotency key where the provider supports one. Where it does not, record "sending" before the call. After a crash, a message found in "sending" is not sent again without a check. That favours a rare missed notification over a duplicate, which matches the requirement. Say so in the design.

**Left out on purpose.** No partitioning: 180 GB fits. No second region: nothing in the requirements asks for it. No strict ordering: notifications to one user may arrive slightly out of order.

steps.title: Which signal to scale on
steps.text: The notification service's workers are autoscaled. Three signals are proposed: the workers' processor use, the number of messages in the queue, and the age of the oldest message in the transactional queue.

steps.title: Where to go next
steps.text:
You can now take a vague request, turn it into requirements and numbers, start from a simple design, and add parts for stated reasons. You can also read someone else's design and find what it cannot survive.

Four habits are worth keeping.

- **Estimate first.** A few minutes of rounded arithmetic settles most arguments about what is needed.
- **Start simple and name the reason for every part you add.**
- **Ask what happens when each part is slow**, not only when it is down.
- **Write down what you gave up.** Every design does give things up, and the next person needs to know which ones were chosen.

The way to improve from here is practice on real systems. Read how the systems you use are built. When something fails, find out which part failed and why the failure spread or did not. Review designs with other people, since they will see what you missed, and you will see what they missed.

questions.prompt: Which fault causes the most harm on the day sales open?

choices.text: The weekly backup
choices.feedback: It matters after a disaster. It does not affect the sale itself.

choices.text: Checking and subtracting the seat count as two separate steps
choices.feedback: Thousands of buyers read "1 seat left" at the same instant and all proceed. Seats are sold many times over, and each of those customers has been charged.

choices.text: The 12 queries per page view
choices.feedback: They make the site slow under load. Overselling is worse, since it takes real money for seats that do not exist.

questions.prompt: Which signal best matches the 10-second requirement?

choices.text: Processor use
choices.feedback: Workers spend most of their time waiting for providers. They can be far behind with idle processors.

choices.text: Queue length
choices.feedback: Length says how much is waiting, and how long that takes depends on how fast it drains. It is a fair second choice.

choices.text: The age of the oldest transactional message
choices.feedback: It measures the thing that was promised. If the oldest message has waited 8 seconds, the target is about to be missed, whatever the other numbers say.

flawed.code:
browsers --> one app server --> one database
                     |
                     +--> email provider (called in the request,
                          no timeout, to send the ticket)

   - seats left are kept in the app server's memory and written
     to the database every 30 seconds
   - buying a ticket: read seats left, if above 0 then subtract 1
     and charge the card
   - the event page is built from 12 database queries on every view
   - if the charge fails, the request is retried at once, 5 times
   - logins are stored in the app server's memory
   - backups: a copy of the database is taken every Sunday
   - expected load: 80,000 people at the moment sales open
